Patient message:
Hi, I'm a 58-year-old man and something happened this morning that caught me off guard. When I went to the bathroom first thing, the toilet water was clearly pink-red. It didn't hurt at all though — no burning, no pain in my back or sides, nothing like that. I went two more times after that and it looked completely normal both times. I feel totally fine otherwise.

A little background on me: I smoked for a while but quit about 10 years ago — probably around a pack a day for 20 years. I take lisinopril for my blood pressure.

I actually went in and got checked out today. My blood pressure was 134/78 and heart rate was 68. The doctor said my belly was soft with no tenderness, and when they tapped on my back and sides there was no pain. No fever either.

Then my lab results just showed up on my patient portal and I'm trying to make sense of them. The urinalysis showed blood marked as "Large" — the reference says it should be negative, so that's flagged abnormal. The red blood cells were 50 to 100 per high-power field, and normal is supposed to be 0 to 2, so that's high. But the white blood cells were 0 to 2, which is within normal range of 0 to 5. Nitrites came back negative, which is normal. And my creatinine was 1.1 mg/dL, which falls in the normal range of 0.7 to 1.3.

So the blood in the urine is obviously not normal, but since it went away and I have no pain, I'm not sure how worried I should be. Do I need to be seen again soon, or is this something that can wait for a regular follow-up appointment?
raw_response:
Disposition: GP_ROUTINE

Clinical reasoning: This is painless visible hematuria in a 58-year-old man with a smoking history. That combination is important because, even though the episode was brief and you feel well, painless hematuria can be a sign of underlying urinary tract pathology, including bladder or kidney issues that need proper evaluation. The normal vitals, absence of pain, and reassuring exam make an acute emergency (like infection, obstruction, or kidney stone complication) unlikely. The urinalysis confirms significant blood but no signs of infection. This does not require emergency care, but it does warrant timely outpatient follow-up and likely referral for further investigation (typically imaging and cystoscopy). Waiting a few days to arrange this is reasonable, but it should not be ignored or delayed for weeks without a plan.

Patient explanation: Even though the blood you saw has stopped and you feel fine, this isn’t something to brush off. Blood in the urine without pain—especially at your age—needs a proper workup to rule out anything serious. The good news is there’s no sign of infection or kidney dysfunction, and nothing suggests you’re in danger right now. The next step is to follow up with your doctor fairly soon (within the next few days) so they can arrange the right tests, often including a scan and a look inside the bladder.

Safety netting: Seek more urgent care (same day or ED) if you develop:
- Persistent or heavy visible blood in the urine (especially with clots)
- Difficulty passing urine or inability to urinate
- New pain in your back, side, or lower abdomen
- Fever, chills, or feeling unwell
- Dizziness or lightheadedness

If none of those occur, make sure you have a follow-up plan in place within the next few days.

Patient message:
Hi, I'm a 27-year-old guy and I wanted to get some guidance on something that's been going on for about the past month. A few times after I have a bowel movement, I've noticed bright red blood on the toilet paper when I wipe. It's not actually in the stool itself, just on the paper. I've been kind of constipated lately and I'll admit I've been straining more than usual. I don't have any belly pain, I haven't seen any dark or black-looking stools, and I haven't lost any weight. As far as I know, nobody in my family has had colon cancer.

I had some bloodwork done and the results just showed up in my patient portal. My hemoglobin came back at 14.4 g/dL, which looks normal against the reference range of 13.5–17.5. MCV was 90 fL, normal per the 80–100 range. And my ferritin was 60 ng/mL, also normal with the range listed as 30–400. My blood pressure at the visit was 122/76 and heart rate was 66, but I haven't had a physical exam yet.

I'm not sure how worried I should be about the bleeding. Do I need to be seen, and how soon?
raw_response:
Disposition: GP_ROUTINE

Clinical reasoning: Intermittent bright red blood on wiping in a young patient with constipation and straining is most consistent with a benign anorectal source such as hemorrhoids or a small anal fissure. The absence of blood mixed in stool, no melena, no abdominal pain, no weight loss, and normal hemoglobin and iron studies all strongly reduce concern for a more serious or proximal cause. This has been going on for a month, so it’s reasonable to have a clinician examine the area and confirm the source, but there are no features suggesting urgent or emergency pathology.

Patient explanation: This pattern of bleeding is very commonly caused by things like hemorrhoids or small tears around the anus, especially when you’ve been constipated and straining. Your normal blood counts are reassuring and there’s nothing in your story that suggests something dangerous or time-sensitive. You should book a routine appointment with a GP in the next few days to a couple of weeks so they can examine you and confirm the cause, and help you treat the constipation so this settles.

In the meantime, focus on softening your stools: increase fiber (diet or supplement), drink plenty of fluids, and avoid straining. That alone often stops the bleeding.

Safety netting: Seek more urgent care if you notice any of the following:
- Blood mixed into the stool or darker/maroon/black stools
- Bleeding becoming heavier, more frequent, or dripping into the toilet
- New abdominal pain, unexplained weight loss, or persistent change in bowel habits
- Feeling dizzy, faint, or signs of anemia (unusual fatigue, shortness of breath)
- If the bleeding continues despite improving constipation over the next few weeks

Otherwise, this can safely wait for a routine GP review.

Patient message:
Hi, I'm a 29-year-old guy and I'm a little freaked out by some lab results that just showed up on my patient portal. Let me back up — about two weeks ago I had some kind of viral bug, nothing major, and I took a few doses of ibuprofen for it. I'm not on any blood thinners and I don't have any liver problems.

Starting about three days ago I noticed a bunch of tiny red and purple dots popping up all over my legs. Then I realized my gums have been bleeding whenever I brush my teeth. Today I got a nosebleed that took a solid 15 minutes to finally stop, which is not normal for me at all.

I went in and they checked me out — my blood pressure was 118/72, heart rate 84, and temperature was 36.7°C, so all normal there. The doctor pointed out scattered petechiae on my legs and also inside my mouth but said there weren't any large bruises anywhere.

Then the labs posted and that's what's really worrying me. My platelet count came back at 38 K/uL, and the reference range says 150 to 400, so that's flagged low. My hemoglobin was 13.8 g/dL which is in the normal range of 13.5 to 17.5. White blood cell count was 6.2 K/uL, normal range 4.0 to 11.0. And my INR was 1.0, normal range 0.9 to 1.1 — so those three are all fine.

I'm pretty concerned about the platelet number being that low combined with the bleeding and the spots. Do I need to be seen again, and how soon?
raw_response:
Disposition: URGENT_CARE

The rest of the blood counts and INR are normal, which makes a primary platelet problem (e.g. post-viral immune thrombocytopenia) more likely than a global bone marrow or clotting disorder. He is currently hemodynamically stable and not reporting severe or ongoing bleeding, so this does not mandate immediate ED-level resuscitation. However, platelets below ~50 with active bleeding carries a meaningful short-term risk of further bleeding and typically warrants prompt reassessment and likely treatment (e.g. steroids) and repeat labs. This should be addressed the same day.

Patient explanation: Your platelet count is quite low, and the spots on your skin plus gum and nose bleeding fit with that. The reassuring part is that your other blood tests and vital signs are normal, which suggests this is isolated to platelets and not a broader blood problem. Still, a count of 38 with active bleeding is not something to sit on. You should be seen again today (same day) for repeat assessment and likely treatment. If your original clinic can see you urgently, contact them; otherwise go to an urgent care or similar same-day service.

Safety netting: Go to the emergency department immediately if you have any of the following:
- Nosebleed or gum bleeding that won’t stop after 10–15 minutes of steady pressure
- Blood in urine or stool, or black stools
- New large or spreading bruises
- Severe headache, vision changes, confusion, or drowsiness
- Vomiting blood or coughing up blood

Until you’re seen, avoid ibuprofen, aspirin, alcohol, and contact sports or injury risk.

Hi, I'm a 31-year-old guy and I'm hoping someone can help me make sense of some lab results that just showed up in my patient portal. Last week I came down with a cold — sore throat, congestion, the usual stuff. The cold itself has mostly cleared up, but I'm still feeling more tired than I'd expect. I don't have a fever or anything like that. I don't have any autoimmune conditions and I'm not on any medications.

I went in for a visit and they said my exam was normal. My blood pressure was 112/68, heart rate 70, and temperature 36.7°C. But when I looked at the labs online, a couple of things were flagged. My white blood cell count came back at 3.3 K/uL, which it says is low — the normal range listed is 4.0 to 11.0. My absolute neutrophil count was 1.5 K/uL, right at the very bottom of the reference range of 1.5 to 7.0, so it's marked as borderline. My hemoglobin was 13.1 g/dL, which looks normal (range 12.0–16.0), and platelets were 220 K/uL, also normal (range 150–400).

I'm not sure how worried I should be about the low white count and the borderline neutrophils, especially since I was just sick. Do I need to be seen again, and how soon?

Hemoglobin and platelets are normal, which is reassuring and argues against a broader bone marrow problem. Transient suppression of white cells, especially neutrophils, is very common after viral infections and typically recovers over days to a few weeks. There are no red flag symptoms (fever, recurrent infections, systemic illness), and the exam and vitals are normal. This does not require urgent or emergency care, but a repeat blood count to confirm recovery is appropriate.

Patient explanation: Your blood results are most consistent with a temporary dip in white blood cells from your recent cold. This happens quite often and usually corrects itself without any treatment. The fact that your other blood counts are normal and you’re otherwise feeling okay is reassuring. You don’t need urgent care, but it would be sensible to follow up with your GP in the next few days to a couple of weeks to repeat the blood test and make sure things are trending back to normal.

Safety netting: Seek more urgent care if you develop a fever (especially ≥38°C), feel acutely unwell, or start getting unusual or recurrent infections (like persistent sore throat, mouth ulcers, or skin infections). Also seek review sooner if your fatigue is worsening rather than improving, or if new symptoms appear such as unexplained bruising, night sweats, or weight loss.

Hi, I'm a 42-year-old man and something pretty alarming happened this morning. When I woke up, the right side of my face felt weak — I noticed it right away because I couldn't fully close my right eye and when I tried to smile in the mirror, the right side of my mouth just drooped. It's not just the lower part of my face either; when I try to raise my eyebrows, the right side barely moves. I want to be clear though, I have no weakness in my arms or legs, no difficulty speaking or understanding what people say to me, and no headache at all.

About a week ago I had a mild cold, but otherwise I've been healthy. No diabetes, no history of stroke or heart disease.

I actually went to an urgent care this morning and they checked me over. My blood pressure was 128/78, heart rate 72, and temperature was 37.0°C. The doctor said the facial weakness was affecting both my forehead and the lower face on the right side, and that my eye wasn't closing all the way. She said there were no other neurological problems found on exam.

Some lab results just posted to my patient portal too. My glucose was 94 mg/dL, which they marked as normal (range 70-100). HbA1c was 5.4%, also normal (range 4.0-5.6). White blood cell count was 7.2 K/uL, normal (4.0-11.0). And my ESR was 12 mm/hr, normal (range 0-22).

I'm honestly a bit scared because I know facial drooping can be a sign of a stroke, but since I don't have any other stroke-like symptoms I'm not sure how worried to be. Do I need to be seen again, and how soon?

Stroke is much less likely when the forehead is involved and there are no limb, speech, or sensory deficits. However, early treatment (typically corticosteroids, ideally within 72 hours of onset) meaningfully improves recovery, and eye protection is important since the eyelid is not closing fully. He has already been assessed once today, but timely follow-up is still important to ensure treatment has been started and to manage eye care.

That’s reassuring. The important thing now is early treatment and protecting your eye. If the urgent care already started you on steroids and gave eye care advice, that’s appropriate. If not, you should arrange to be seen again today or tomorrow to start treatment within the first couple of days.

Safety netting: Seek immediate care (ED) if you develop any of the following: weakness in your arm or leg, trouble speaking or understanding speech, severe headache, double vision, loss of balance, or if the facial weakness rapidly worsens beyond what you’ve already noticed. Also seek urgent review if you cannot keep your eye moist despite drops, develop eye pain or redness, or if new symptoms appear that don’t fit the current pattern.

Patient message:
Hi, I'm a 35-year-old male and I'm hoping to get some guidance on what's going on with my left eye. Starting about two days ago it got really red, painful, and extremely sensitive to light. The pain feels like a deep ache from inside the eye rather than a scratchy or foreign-body feeling. My vision in that eye also seems a little blurry. There's no discharge or crusting at all.

I don't have any history of eye problems besides needing glasses, no autoimmune conditions that I'm aware of, and I don't wear contacts.

I was seen and they checked my vitals — blood pressure was 118/74, heart rate 68, and temperature 36.8°C. On exam they said my left eye is red especially around the colored part of the eye, and that my left pupil looks a bit smaller than the right. No discharge was seen. They tested my vision and it was 20/30 in the left eye, which is usually 20/20 with my glasses.

I also just got some lab results posted to my patient portal. My white blood cell count was 6.8 K/uL, which is in the normal range of 4.0–11.0. ESR was 18 mm/hr, normal range 0–20. CRP was 3.2 mg/L with a reference of less than 5, so that's normal too. And the ANA came back negative.

Everything in the labs looks normal from what I can tell, but my eye is really bothering me and I'm worried about the vision change. Do I need to be seen, and how soon?
raw_response:
Disposition: URGENT_CARE

Clinical reasoning: This is a classic pattern for anterior uveitis (iritis): deep aching eye pain, marked light sensitivity, blurred vision, redness concentrated around the iris (ciliary flush), and a smaller pupil on the affected side. The absence of discharge makes infection like conjunctivitis unlikely. Normal labs do not rule this out and are not particularly helpful for triage here. This condition is not usually an emergency in the next few hours, but it does require prompt (same day or next day) assessment by someone who can examine the eye with a slit lamp and start treatment (typically anti-inflammatory drops, sometimes dilating drops). Delay beyond 24–48 hours can increase the risk of complications and longer-term vision issues.

Patient explanation: You do need to be seen, but this doesn’t need an ER visit right now. Your symptoms strongly suggest inflammation inside the eye, which needs prompt treatment to protect your vision. You should arrange an urgent eye assessment today if possible, or within 24 hours at the latest—ideally with an optometrist or ophthalmologist rather than general urgent care.

Safety netting: Go to the emergency department immediately if any of the following happen: rapidly worsening vision, severe increase in pain, new headache with nausea/vomiting, seeing halos around lights, the eye becoming very hard to open, or if you cannot access urgent eye care within 24 hours.

Hi, I'm a 62-year-old man and I just got some results on my patient portal that I'm trying to make sense of. For about the past week I've been getting this pressure feeling in my chest whenever I walk up a hill. It goes away if I stop and rest for a few minutes, and it's never happened when I'm just sitting around. Right now I feel completely fine, no chest pain at all. I don't get any pain in my jaw or arm with it, no nausea, no sweating or anything like that.

Some background on me — I have type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, and high cholesterol. I take metformin, lisinopril, and atorvastatin for those. When they checked me, my blood pressure was 142/88, heart rate 78, and my oxygen was 98% on room air. They did an EKG and said it showed normal rhythm with some nonspecific ST-T changes, but they told me it looks the same as the one I had done about six months ago.

The labs that just posted to my portal are: troponin less than 0.01 ng/mL, which it says is normal (reference under 0.04); BNP 45 pg/mL, also normal (reference under 100); glucose 142 mg/dL, flagged high (normal range 70–100); and creatinine 1.0 mg/dL, normal (reference 0.7–1.3).

I'm not sure how worried I should be about the chest pressure I've been having, especially with everything else going on. Do I need to be seen, and how soon?
raw_response:

Clinical reasoning: This is a very typical story for exertional angina — chest pressure reliably brought on by exertion and relieved by rest — in a 62-year-old with multiple cardiovascular risk factors (diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia). The normal troponin and stable EKG are reassuring that there is no evidence of an ongoing heart attack right now, and the fact that symptoms stop with rest suggests a stable pattern rather than an immediately unstable one. However, this still represents a meaningful risk of underlying coronary artery disease that needs prompt evaluation and management. The short-term risk is not zero, and early assessment (within 24 hours) can reduce the chance of progression to an acute event. Emergency department care is not necessary at this moment because he is pain-free, stable, and has no signs of ongoing ischemia, but waiting several days would be inappropriate.

Patient explanation: What you’re describing sounds very much like “angina,” which is when the heart isn’t getting quite enough blood flow during exertion. The fact that it comes on with walking uphill and goes away with rest is a key pattern. Your tests so far are reassuring that nothing acute is happening right now, but this still needs to be checked promptly. You should be seen within the next day (for example, urgent primary care or cardiology), as they may want to arrange further testing like a stress test or adjust your medications.

Safety netting: Go to the emergency department immediately if:
- The chest pressure happens at rest or lasts longer than 10–15 minutes
- The pain becomes more frequent, more severe, or happens with less activity than before
- You develop associated symptoms like shortness of breath, sweating, nausea, dizziness, or pain spreading to the arm, jaw, or back
- You feel faint or unwell in a new way

If your current pattern stays the same (only with exertion, relieved by rest), still make sure you are seen within 24 hours.

Patient message:
Hi, I'm a 52-year-old man and I'm trying to figure out how worried I should be about some things going on with me. For about the last two weeks my lower back has been aching. There wasn't any injury or anything that set it off — it just started. The thing that bothers me most is that it's worse at night and actually wakes me up sometimes. On top of that I've been having night sweats and I've lost around 8 pounds without trying to. I don't have any weakness or numbness in my legs, and my bowels and bladder are working fine. I used to smoke but I quit about 5 years ago.

I had a visit recently and they checked my vitals — blood pressure was 118/74, heart rate 76, temperature 99.1°F, and oxygen was 98%. The doctor said my back was tender when they pressed on it but my neurological exam was normal, strength and sensation both okay.

Then some labs just posted to my patient portal and a couple of them are flagged. My white blood cell count was 9.8, which looks normal. But my hemoglobin came back at 11.8 g/dL and it says the normal range starts at 12, so it's a little low. The one that really caught my eye is my ESR — it was 48 mm/hr and the reference range says it should be under 20, so that's pretty high. My CRP was also high at 2.8 mg/dL when it's supposed to be under 0.5.

With the back pain waking me up at night, the weight loss, the night sweats, and now these lab results, I'm getting anxious. Do I need to be seen, and how soon?
raw_response:
Disposition: URGENT_CARE

The combination of persistent back pain without a clear trigger, pain waking you at night, unintentional weight loss, night sweats, mild anemia, and significantly elevated ESR/CRP raises concern for an underlying systemic process such as malignancy (including metastatic disease or myeloma) or spinal infection. You are currently stable (normal vitals, no neurological deficits, no bowel/bladder symptoms), which argues against an immediate emergency requiring ED-level intervention in the next few hours. However, the pattern is concerning enough that waiting several days would be inappropriate — you need prompt in-person reassessment and likely imaging and further blood tests.

Patient explanation: You’re right to take this seriously. Most back pain is benign, but your symptoms and lab results aren’t the usual pattern. This doesn’t mean something dangerous is definitely happening, but it does mean we shouldn’t wait. You should be seen again urgently — ideally within 24 hours — to arrange further tests (often imaging like an MRI and more blood work) to figure out what’s causing this.

Safety netting: Go to the emergency department immediately if you develop:
- New weakness, numbness, or tingling in your legs
- Trouble walking or standing
- Loss of bowel or bladder control
- Severe, rapidly worsening back pain
- Fever (especially >100.4°F / 38°C) or feeling acutely unwell
- Pain that becomes constant and unbearable despite rest or medication

If none of those occur, still arrange urgent follow-up within a day.

Hi, I'm a 36-year-old guy with asthma, though I haven't had to go to the ER for it in years. Starting about 12 hours ago I've been dealing with wheezing and chest tightness that keeps coming back. The doctor noted wheezing throughout both lungs but said there was no bluish color to my lips or skin and I wasn't using my neck muscles to breathe.

My peak flow came back at 320 L/min, which is low — my personal best is around 520. The venous blood gas showed a pH of 7.36, which they said is normal (range 7.35–7.45), but the pCO2 was 46 mmHg, a little above the normal range of 35–45. White blood cell count was 10.8 x10^3/uL, which looks like it's at the high end of normal (4.5–11.0).

I'm not sure what to make of all this together. Do I need to be seen again, and how soon?

The trajectory over 12 hours suggests ongoing bronchospasm that is not adequately controlled with home treatment. The emergency setting can provide repeated/nebulized bronchodilators, systemic steroids, oxygen, and close monitoring with the ability to escalate quickly if you worsen.

Patient explanation: You’re having a significant asthma flare that isn’t settling with your inhaler, and some of your numbers suggest your lungs are starting to struggle rather than compensate. Even though you can still speak comfortably, this is the kind of situation that can turn more serious over the next several hours. You should go to the emergency department now to get stronger treatment and monitoring.

Safety netting: Go immediately, but if anything worsens on the way — increasing breathlessness, difficulty speaking full sentences, feeling drowsy or exhausted, chest “silent” with less wheeze, lips/fingertips turning bluish, or needing your inhaler more frequently than every 2–3 hours with little effect — treat that as urgent and seek immediate help (call emergency services if needed).

Hi, I'm a 45-year-old man and something weird has been happening this week that I wanted to ask about. Twice now, my entire left arm has gone numb and tingly — both times it lasted around 15 minutes and then went away completely. During the episodes there was no weakness in the arm or anywhere else, my face wasn't drooping, and my speech was totally fine. Right now I feel completely normal, like nothing happened. For background, I don't smoke, I don't have diabetes or high blood pressure, and I'm not on any blood thinners or really any medications. I'm not sure if this is something I should be worried about or not. Do I need to be seen, and if so, how soon?
raw_response:
Disposition: URGENT_CARE

Clinical reasoning: Two brief, fully resolving episodes of unilateral arm numbness raise concern for a transient neurological event such as a TIA, even in the absence of weakness or speech disturbance. While this is not an active emergency right now (symptoms have resolved and no ongoing deficit), the pattern is focal, recurrent, and vascular until proven otherwise. The short-term risk of a more serious event (e.g. stroke) is highest in the first 24–48 hours after such episodes, and timely assessment (including imaging and possibly starting preventative treatment) meaningfully reduces that risk. This is not something that should wait several days, but it does not require immediate ED care if rapid same-day evaluation is accessible.

Patient explanation: What you’re describing isn’t something to ignore. Even though the symptoms went away and you feel normal now, brief episodes of one-sided numbness can sometimes be warning signs of a circulation issue to the brain. The good news is you’re currently well, but this still needs to be checked promptly—ideally today or within 24 hours. If you can access urgent same-day care (your GP urgently, urgent care clinic, or a stroke/TIA clinic), that’s appropriate. If that’s not possible, going to the emergency department is reasonable.

Safety netting: Seek immediate emergency care (call emergency services) if:
- The numbness returns, especially if it lasts longer or doesn’t fully resolve
- You develop weakness, clumsiness, or dropping things in that arm
- Any facial drooping, slurred speech, trouble finding words, or vision problems occur
- You feel dizzy, unsteady, or develop a severe headache

Even if symptoms are mild or brief, recurrence should push you to emergency care rather than waiting.

Hi, I'm a 59-year-old man and I just had some routine bloodwork done. I have a history of high blood pressure and chronic kidney disease. Honestly I feel mostly fine — the only thing I've noticed is maybe some mild muscle cramps in my legs, nothing too alarming. I'm just trying to figure out if there's anything in these results I should be worried about and whether I need to do anything right away. Do I need to be seen, and how soon?
raw_response:
Disposition: URGENT_CARE

Clinical reasoning: A 59-year-old with chronic kidney disease and hypertension who has had recent bloodwork but does not provide the results introduces significant uncertainty. In CKD, routine labs can reveal electrolyte disturbances (especially potassium, calcium, or bicarbonate) or worsening kidney function that may require prompt adjustment of medications or treatment. Mild muscle cramps could be benign, but in this context they can also be an early symptom of electrolyte imbalance. Hi, I'm a 47-year-old male and I'm a little worried about my left leg. I don't have any history of blood clots or clotting problems, and I'm not on any blood thinners. I've been reading some stuff online about clots after long flights and it's making me nervous. Do I need to be seen, and how soon?

He is currently stable with no chest pain or shortness of breath, so there’s no sign of a pulmonary embolism right now, which keeps this out of ED_NOW. However, the risk of clot propagation or embolization over the next 24–48 hours is real, and diagnosis (typically ultrasound) and treatment should not be delayed. Same-day or next-day in-person assessment is appropriate.

Patient explanation: You’re right to take this seriously. A swollen, painful calf after a long flight can be a blood clot in the leg, and that’s something we should check promptly. You don’t need to rush to the emergency department right this minute since you’re otherwise feeling well, but you should be seen today or within the next 24 hours for an exam and likely an ultrasound.

Safety netting: If you develop any chest pain, shortness of breath, coughing up blood, feeling faint, or a rapid heartbeat, go to the emergency department immediately — those can be signs the clot has moved to the lungs. Also seek urgent care if the leg swelling rapidly worsens, becomes very tense, or you develop significant new pain.

Hi, I'm a 23-year-old guy with type 1 diabetes and I'm having a rough day. Since this morning I've been incredibly thirsty — like I can't drink enough water — and I've been running to the bathroom to pee constantly. I also feel a little nauseous and my stomach is kind of achy, though it's not terrible. I'm not confused or anything, and I can still keep small sips of water down, so that's something. I don't have a fever either. I know with my diabetes these kinds of symptoms can sometimes mean something more serious is going on, but I'm not sure how worried I should be right now. Disposition: ED_NOW

Even though you are currently alert and able to drink, this can be an early or partially compensated phase. DKA can worsen over hours, and early treatment (fluids, insulin, blood tests to check glucose, ketones, and electrolytes) significantly reduces risk. This is not something that can be safely assessed or managed at home or delayed to routine care.

Patient explanation: Your symptoms fit a pattern we take seriously in type 1 diabetes because they can signal your body is becoming acidotic. Even if it feels mild right now, this can escalate fairly quickly. You should go to the emergency department now so they can check your blood sugar, ketones, and start treatment if needed.

Safety netting: Go immediately. If you develop vomiting, worsening abdominal pain, rapid or deep breathing, confusion, drowsiness, or you’re unable to keep fluids down, treat that as even more urgent and seek help right away (call emergency services if needed).

I'm not throwing up and I don't feel lightheaded or faint or anything like that. I do have this mild indigestion-type feeling in my upper stomach area, but it's honestly not that bad — more of a dull discomfort than real pain. The key issue is that this may require prompt blood tests, monitoring, and possibly endoscopic treatment—things only available in an emergency setting in the short term. The short-term trajectory is uncertain: some patients remain stable, but others can deteriorate over hours if bleeding continues.

Patient explanation: What you’re describing—black, tar-like stool—is concerning for bleeding somewhere in your upper digestive tract. The ibuprofen use makes that more likely. Even though you feel okay right now, this isn’t something to watch at home. You should go to the emergency department today so they can check your blood count, assess whether bleeding is ongoing, and treat it if needed.

Safety netting: Go immediately (call emergency services rather than driving yourself) if you develop:
- Lightheadedness, fainting, or weakness  
- Vomiting blood or material that looks like coffee grounds  
- Rapid heartbeat or shortness of breath  
- Worsening abdominal pain  
- Passing more black stools or any red blood  

Even if none of these happen, you should still go to the ED now for evaluation.

It didn't hurt at all — no burning, no pain in my back or sides, nothing like that. I've gone twice more since then and everything looks completely normal again. I feel fine otherwise, no other symptoms. For background, I used to be a smoker but I quit about 10 years ago — probably smoked about a pack a day for 20 years or so. The only medication I'm on is lisinopril for my blood pressure. I wasn't sure if one episode of blood in the urine like that is something I need to get checked out right away or if it can wait for a regular appointment. Do I need to be seen, and how soon?
raw_response:
Disposition: GP_ROUTINE

Clinical reasoning: A single episode of painless visible blood in the urine in a 58-year-old man, especially with a past smoking history, is significant even if it resolved and you feel well. The most likely causes include things like a transient bleed from the urinary tract, infection, or prostate issues, but the most important “don’t miss” cause is a urinary tract malignancy (e.g., bladder or kidney), which can present exactly like this—painless and intermittent. You are currently stable, with no ongoing bleeding, pain, or systemic symptoms, so there is no indication for emergency care. However, this does warrant prompt outpatient evaluation (typically imaging and a urology referral), and it should not be left to drift.

Patient explanation: Even though it only happened once and went away, visible blood in the urine should always be checked out—especially at your age. It doesn’t mean something serious is definitely going on, but it’s important to rule out causes that need treatment. You don’t need to go to the emergency department, but you should book an appointment with your GP in the next few days so they can start the appropriate tests and referral.

Safety netting: Seek more urgent care (same day or ED) if:
- The blood in your urine returns and is heavy or persistent
- You develop pain in your back, sides, or lower abdomen
- You have difficulty passing urine or cannot pass urine
- You develop fever, chills, or feel unwell
- You notice clots in the urine or worsening urinary symptoms

If none of those occur, still make sure you’re seen soon for proper evaluation.

Hi, I'm a 27-year-old guy and I've been noticing something that's got me a little worried. For about the past month, every now and then after I have a bowel movement I'll see bright red blood on the toilet paper when I wipe. It's not actually in the stool itself, just on the paper. I've also been pretty constipated lately and find myself straining more than usual. I don't have any belly pain, and I haven't noticed any dark or black-looking stools. My weight has been stable too. As far as I know, nobody in my family has had colon cancer or anything like that. I'm not sure if this is something minor or if I should be more concerned. Do I need to be seen, and how soon?

The absence of blood mixed in stool, black stools, weight loss, or abdominal pain is reassuring. This has been ongoing for a month, so it’s not purely transient, and a routine clinical review is reasonable to confirm the source and guide treatment. There are no features suggesting a need for urgent or emergency evaluation.

Patient explanation: This pattern is very commonly caused by things like hemorrhoids or a small tear at the edge of the anus, especially when you’re constipated and straining. It’s unlikely to be anything serious based on what you’ve described. That said, since it’s been happening for a few weeks, it’s sensible to see a GP in the next few days to get it checked and get advice on treatment—often simple measures can sort it out.

In the meantime, focusing on relieving constipation will help: drink plenty of fluids, increase fiber (fruit, veg, whole grains or a fiber supplement), and avoid straining.

Safety netting: Seek more urgent care if you notice any of the following:
- Blood mixed into the stool rather than just on wiping
- Black or tarry stools
- Increasing or heavy bleeding
- New abdominal pain, especially persistent or severe
- Unexplained weight loss, fatigue, or change in bowel habits lasting several weeks
- Feeling dizzy or faint with bleeding

If the bleeding continues despite improving constipation, or doesn’t settle over the next few weeks, make sure you follow up.

This does not require emergency or same-day care, but it does warrant timely in-person assessment, ideally within the next few weeks, for examination and possible dermoscopy or biopsy.

Patient explanation: This is worth getting checked, but it’s not an emergency. Changes in size and color over time are exactly the kind of things we like to look at more closely. Book a routine appointment with your GP or a skin specialist in the next couple of weeks so they can examine it properly.

Safety netting: Seek more urgent review if you notice rapid change (over days to weeks), irregular or spreading borders, multiple colors developing, bleeding, crusting, itching, or pain, or if new similar lesions appear.

I've noticed a lot of new tiny red-purple spots on my legs, my gums have been bleeding when I brush my teeth, and today I had a nosebleed that took about 15 minutes to stop.

About two weeks ago I had a viral illness. I'm not on blood thinners and I don't have liver disease. The only medicine I took was a few doses of ibuprofen.

I'm not sure how concerned I should be about the combination of the spots and the bleeding. Do I need to get checked today, or can this wait?

This pattern indicates impaired clotting and carries a real risk of more serious bleeding, including internal bleeding, even if you currently feel otherwise well. This isn’t just “worth checking soon” — it needs same-day blood testing and the ability to act immediately on results (e.g., very low platelets may require urgent treatment or monitoring), which is best handled in an emergency setting.

Patient explanation: The spots and bleeding you’re describing together are not typical minor symptoms — they suggest your blood may not be clotting properly. This can sometimes happen after a viral illness. You need to be checked today with urgent blood tests to see your platelet level and make sure you’re not at risk of more serious bleeding. The safest place to do that quickly is the emergency department.

Safety netting: Go now rather than waiting. If, while waiting or en route, you develop severe headache, vision changes, confusion, blood in urine or stool, vomiting blood, worsening or uncontrollable bleeding, or large new bruises, alert medical staff immediately.

Hi, I'm a 42-year-old man and something pretty alarming happened this morning. When I woke up, the right side of my face felt weak — I noticed I can't fully close my right eye, and when I tried to smile in the mirror the right corner of my mouth just droops down. It's really only my face though. My arms and legs feel totally normal, I'm not having any trouble talking or understanding what people say to me, and I don't have a headache or anything like that. The only thing I can think of is that I had a mild cold about a week ago, but otherwise I've been healthy. I don't have diabetes, and no history of stroke or heart disease. I'm honestly a little freaked out because anything with the face makes you think of a stroke, but since it's just the one side of my face and nothing else, I'm not sure how worried I should be. Do I need to be seen today, or can this wait for a regular doctor's appointment?
raw_response:
Disposition: URGENT_CARE

Clinical reasoning: Acute onset unilateral facial weakness involving the eye (inability to fully close it) and mouth strongly suggests a peripheral facial nerve palsy (e.g., Bell’s palsy), especially with recent viral illness and no other neurological deficits. The absence of arm/leg weakness, speech disturbance, or confusion lowers the likelihood of stroke, but does not completely eliminate it without examination. Early treatment (typically steroids) is most effective if started within 72 hours, so same-day assessment is important. This does not currently require emergency department resources given the isolated symptoms and stable condition.

Patient explanation:  
What you’re describing sounds most consistent with Bell’s palsy, which is a temporary weakness of one side of the face and often happens after a viral illness. The fact that you can’t fully close your eye on that side is actually a key clue that points away from a stroke and toward this diagnosis.  

That said, you should be seen today (urgent care or same-day GP) so someone can confirm the diagnosis and start treatment if appropriate. Starting medication early can improve recovery.

Safety netting:  
Go to the emergency department immediately if you develop:
- Weakness or numbness in your arm or leg  
- Trouble speaking, understanding, or confusion  
- Severe headache, dizziness, or loss of balance  
- Vision problems beyond the eye not closing  
- Symptoms spreading beyond just your face  

Also, protect your eye in the meantime (since it’s not closing fully): consider using lubricating eye drops and avoid letting it dry out.

Hi, I'm a 62-year-old man and I wanted to ask about something that's been going on for about a week now. Whenever I walk up a hill or do something that takes a bit of effort, I get this pressure feeling in my chest. It's not sharp or anything, more like a heavy sensation. Once I stop and rest for a few minutes it goes away completely. It's never happened when I'm just sitting around or at rest, and right now as I'm typing this I feel perfectly fine with no chest pain at all. I don't get any pain in my jaw or arm with it, no nausea, and no sweating either. For background, I have type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, and high cholesterol, and I take metformin, lisinopril, and atorvastatin for those. I'm not sure if this is something I need to get checked out soon or if it can wait for a regular appointment — do I need to be seen, and how soon?
raw_response:
Disposition: URGENT_CARE

Clinical reasoning: This is a very typical pattern of exertional chest pressure that reliably comes on with effort and resolves with rest in a 62-year-old with diabetes, hypertension, and high cholesterol. The most likely explanation is stable angina (reduced blood flow to the heart during exertion). While you are currently pain-free and not showing features of an acute heart attack, this pattern indicates a significant risk of coronary artery disease that needs prompt evaluation. The short-term risk is not zero—stable angina can progress or destabilize—so waiting several days would not be appropriate. However, there is no indication right now that you need emergency department care since symptoms are predictable, short-lived, and only with exertion.

Patient explanation: The symptoms you’re describing are concerning for strain on the heart during activity, most often due to narrowed heart arteries. Because of your age and medical history, this needs to be checked soon—ideally today or within the next 24 hours—so a clinician can assess you, run tests (like an ECG and possibly blood tests or a stress test), and start treatment if needed. Since you’re comfortable at rest and the symptoms go away quickly, this does not sound like an emergency right this moment, but it should not be delayed.

Safety netting: Go to the emergency department immediately if:
- The chest pressure happens at rest or wakes you from sleep
- The pain lasts longer than 10–15 minutes or does not go away with rest
- The episodes become more frequent, more severe, or happen with less activity
- You develop shortness of breath, sweating, nausea, dizziness, or pain spreading to the arm, jaw, neck, or back

Until you’re seen, avoid heavy exertion that brings on symptoms.

What's been bothering me the most is that it gets noticeably worse at night, to the point where it actually wakes me up from sleep. On top of that, I've been having night sweats and I've dropped around 8 pounds recently without changing my diet or exercise at all. I don't have any weakness or numbness in my legs, and my bowel and bladder are working fine. For what it's worth, I used to smoke but I quit about 5 years ago. The combination of persistent back pain without a clear trigger, pain that is worse at night and wakes you from sleep, unintentional weight loss, and night sweats are “red flag” features. These raise concern for underlying causes such as malignancy or infection rather than a benign musculoskeletal strain. You are currently stable with no neurological deficits or bowel/bladder changes, so there is no clear need for emergency department care in the next few hours. However, the pattern is concerning enough that it should be assessed promptly, with examination and likely imaging and blood tests, ideally within 24 hours.

Patient explanation: You’re right to be concerned, and this isn’t something I’d brush off as routine back pain. The night pain, weight loss, and sweats together mean you should be checked fairly quickly. You don’t need to rush to the ER right now, but you should arrange to be seen urgently—today or tomorrow—by a doctor who can examine you and organize tests.

Safety netting: Go to the emergency department immediately if you develop:
- New weakness, numbness, or difficulty walking
- Loss of bowel or bladder control
- Severe, rapidly worsening pain
- Fever or feeling acutely unwell
- Pain that becomes unbearable or constant despite rest

If you can’t get a timely urgent appointment, or symptoms are progressing over the next day or two, escalate to urgent/emergency care.

Patient message:
Hi, I'm a 35-year-old man and I woke up this morning with a headache that's been going on about 8 hours now. It came on gradually over the first hour and feels like a tight band of pressure all the way around my head. I don't usually get headaches, and this is the worst one I've had.

I don't have a fever, my neck isn't stiff, my vision seems normal, and I haven't had weakness, numbness, or vomiting. I don't have any known medical problems.

I'm not sure whether this is something that can wait or whether I should get checked sooner. Do I need to be seen, and how soon?
raw_response:
Disposition: GP_ROUTINE

Clinical reasoning: The headache description is most consistent with a tension-type headache: gradual onset, “tight band” quality, no neurological symptoms, no fever or meningism. The fact that it is your worst headache does raise the level of attention, but the absence of red flags such as sudden (thunderclap) onset, focal deficits, altered consciousness, or systemic symptoms makes an acute dangerous cause much less likely. Over the next 24–48 hours, this is more likely to remain stable or improve than to deteriorate abruptly. There is no clear benefit from emergency department care right now, but given that this is unusual for you and relatively severe, a routine GP review is reasonable if it doesn’t settle.

Patient explanation: This sounds like a tension-style headache, which can feel quite intense even if it’s not dangerous. Based on what you’ve described, you don’t need to go to the emergency department right now. You can try simple measures like rest, hydration, and over-the-counter pain relief (such as paracetamol or ibuprofen if you can take them safely). If it’s not improving over the next day or two, or if you’re concerned, it would be sensible to see your GP.

Safety netting: Seek urgent care (same day or ED) if any of the following happen:
- The headache suddenly becomes very severe (“hits like a bolt” rather than gradual)
- You develop weakness, numbness, trouble speaking, confusion, or vision changes
- You get a fever, stiff neck, or sensitivity to light
- You start vomiting repeatedly
- The pain keeps worsening despite pain relief or is still severe after 48 hours

If anything feels significantly different or worrying compared to what you’ve described, err on the side of getting checked sooner.

Hi, I'm a 22-year-old guy and I'm trying to figure out if I need to do something about this belly pain. Since yesterday I've had this dull ache on the lower right side of my stomach — I'd say maybe a 5 out of 10. I've been feeling a bit queasy but I haven't actually thrown up. My appetite has been kind of off too. For context, I had a stomach bug about a week ago that mostly cleared up on its own. I don't have any burning when I pee or anything like that, and I've never had any surgeries before. I'm not sure if this is just leftover stuff from being sick last week or something I should worry about. Do I need to get checked today, or can this wait?

Disposition: URGENT_CARE

However, appendicitis can evolve over hours, and early assessment (exam, possibly labs/imaging) is important to avoid progression to perforation. Waiting several days would carry avoidable risk, so same-day or next-day evaluation is appropriate.

Patient explanation: This isn’t something to ignore or wait out for a few days. The location and pattern of your pain could be an early appendix issue, which often starts off mild like this. You don’t necessarily need the emergency department right this minute, but you should be seen today—either urgent care or a same-day GP appointment—to get examined.

Safety netting: Go to the emergency department immediately if any of the following happen:
- Pain becomes sharp, severe, or clearly worsening
- Pain spreads or becomes more constant, especially with movement or walking
- You develop a fever
- You start vomiting or can’t keep fluids down
- Your abdomen becomes very tender, especially if you can’t tolerate touch
- You feel faint, weak, or significantly worse overall

If none of those happen, still get checked today.

- You feel short of breath with the episodes

- You notice a very fast or irregular heartbeat that doesn’t settle quickly

I also have a mild dry cough but no fever. You are still speaking in full sentences and not in obvious distress, which argues against immediate emergency-level instability, but the trajectory could worsen over the next 12–24 hours if untreated. Same-day assessment is appropriate to prevent deterioration.

You should be seen today—urgent care, same-day GP, or similar—so they can assess your breathing and likely start additional treatment to get this under control.

- You’re struggling to speak full sentences or getting breathless at rest
- Your inhaler stops helping, or you need it more often than every 2 hours
- Chest tightness or wheezing is rapidly worsening
- You feel drowsy, exhausted, or lightheaded
- Lips or fingertips look bluish

If things stay as they are but don’t improve, still get seen today.

Patient message:
Hi, I'm a 41-year-old man and I'm reaching out because I've been struggling more than usual over the past month. I've been feeling really depressed and hopeless — more so than my baseline — and a few times I've caught myself having thoughts like "I kind of wish I just wouldn't wake up." I want to be clear though: I don't have any plan to hurt myself and I don't actually want to die. I'm still going to work and taking care of my kids every day, but honestly it's been getting harder and harder to keep that up.

I did bring all of this up with my doctor already. I don't have access to any guns, and I'm not stockpiling medications or anything like that. I have a partner and family who live nearby, and I would reach out to them if things got worse. My doctor had me do a PHQ-9 questionnaire and I scored a 19. I don't drink or use any drugs.

They checked my vitals at the visit — blood pressure was 126/78, heart rate 76, and temperature 98.6. The doctor noted I was cooperative, speaking normally, and oriented, so the exam was apparently fine.

Then a bunch of lab results just showed up in my patient portal and everything looks like it's in the normal range, but I figured I'd share them:
- TSH was 2.6 µIU/mL (reference 0.4–4.0)
- Vitamin B12 was 430 pg/mL (reference 200–900)
- Hemoglobin 14.9 g/dL (reference 13.5–17.5)
- White blood cell count 6.9 x10^3/µL (reference 4.5–11.0)
- Sodium 139 mEq/L (reference 136–145)
- Potassium 4.1 mEq/L (reference 3.5–5.0)
- Creatinine 0.9 mg/dL (reference 0.7–1.3)
- Glucose 96 mg/dL (reference 70–100)

So the labs seem okay, but I'm still feeling pretty rough and those passive thoughts have me worried. Do I need to be seen, and how soon?
raw_response:
Disposition: URGENT_CARE

Clinical reasoning: This is moderately severe depression (PHQ-9 of 19) with persistent symptoms over a month and the presence of passive death wishes (“wish I wouldn’t wake up”). While there is no active plan or intent, no means access, and there are clear protective factors (family, insight, help-seeking, ongoing function), the trajectory is worsening and the emergence of passive suicidal thoughts increases short-term risk compared to baseline depression. This is not an emergency right now because there is no imminent intent or loss of control, but it does warrant prompt follow-up—ideally within the next few days—to reassess risk, adjust or initiate treatment, and put supports in place. Normal labs and vitals reduce concern for a medical driver but don’t change the mental health urgency.

Patient explanation: Thanks for explaining all of that so clearly. What you’re describing is important, and it’s good you reached out. Even though you don’t have any plan to harm yourself, those “not wanting to wake up” thoughts and the fact things are getting harder mean you should be seen again soon—ideally within the next few days. This could be with your GP or a mental health clinician to review treatment options (therapy, medication, or both) and make a plan to help you feel more stable. You don’t need the emergency department right now based on what you’ve said, but this shouldn’t be left to drift.

Safety netting: Seek urgent help (same day or emergency care) if any of the following happen:
- Thoughts shift from passive to active (thinking about harming yourself, making a plan, or feeling like you might act on it)
- You feel unable to keep yourself safe or feel out of control
- You start withdrawing significantly from work, family, or daily responsibilities
- Sleep drops off severely, or anxiety/agitation spikes
- You begin using alcohol or substances to cope

If things worsen suddenly, contact local emergency services or a crisis line right away. Otherwise, arrange a follow-up appointment within a few days and consider telling your partner or a trusted person how you’ve been feeling so you’re not carrying this alone.

Hi, I'm a 45-year-old male and I wanted to get some guidance on something that's been happening this week. Twice now, my entire left arm has gone numb and tingly — each time it lasted about 15 minutes and then went away completely. During the episodes there was no weakness in the arm, my face didn't droop, and my speech was totally fine. Right now I feel perfectly normal.

Some background: I don't smoke, I don't have diabetes or high blood pressure, and I'm not on any blood thinners.

I actually went into the clinic today and they checked me over. My blood pressure was 128/82 and my heart rate was 72 and regular. The doctor did a neurological exam and said everything looked normal. My lab results also just showed up on my patient portal — glucose was 94 mg/dL (reference range 70–100, so normal) and total cholesterol was 198 mg/dL (reference is under 200, also normal).

I'm relieved the exam and labs came back okay, but the episodes themselves still worry me. Do I need to be seen again, and how soon should I follow up?
raw_response:
Disposition: URGENT_CARE

Clinical reasoning: Two brief, fully resolving episodes of numbness/tingling involving the entire left arm are transient focal neurologic symptoms. Benign explanations such as nerve compression or migraine are possible, but a TIA is an important dangerous possibility, and a normal neurologic exam after the episode plus normal glucose/cholesterol do not rule that out. Because the episodes were recurrent this week, this should be assessed promptly, ideally the same day or within 24 hours, since urgent evaluation can lead to ECG/imaging and early stroke-prevention treatment if needed. He is currently completely back to normal with no objective deficits, so ED-level care is not clearly required this minute if urgent follow-up is available, but waiting several days would not be appropriate.

Patient explanation: Yes — I do think you should be followed up again promptly, today if possible or within 24 hours at the latest. The fact that you feel normal now and your office exam/labs were normal is reassuring, but it does not fully rule out a short-lived neurologic event, because those can leave a normal exam once the symptoms have passed. Please contact the clinic that saw you and let them know you had two 15-minute episodes of one-sided arm numbness/tingling and need urgent review, ideally through a TIA/stroke or neurology pathway; if they cannot arrange that promptly, go to the emergency department.

Safety netting: Seek emergency care immediately / call emergency services if the numbness happens again before you are assessed, if it lasts longer than before, does not fully clear, or if you develop any weakness, clumsiness, facial droop, trouble speaking or understanding, vision loss or double vision, severe sudden headache, trouble walking, chest pain, shortness of breath, or fainting.

Hi, I'm a 47-year-old man and I'm trying to figure out how urgently I need to deal with this. For the last two days my left calf has been swollen and sore, and I first noticed it after a six-hour flight. It's definitely more swollen than the other leg. I don't have chest pain or shortness of breath.

I don't have any known clotting disorder and I'm not on blood thinners. When I got checked, my blood pressure was 124/76, heart rate 88, oxygen 98%, and temperature 98.7°F. They noted that the left calf was tender and about 2 cm larger than the right. The skin wasn't very red, and my foot was warm with normal pulses.

My portal labs just came back and the D-dimer was 680 ng/mL FEU, which was flagged high since the reference says under 500. The other labs looked normal: white count 7.1, hemoglobin 14.6, and platelets 240.

Between the calf swelling after the flight and the elevated D-dimer, I'm worried about a blood clot. Do I need to be seen again, and how soon?
raw_response:
Disposition: URGENT_CARE

His normal oxygen level, heart rate, blood pressure, warm foot, and lack of chest pain or shortness of breath are reassuring against a current pulmonary embolism, limb-threatening ischemia, or sepsis, so there is not a clear reason he needs emergency-department-level care this minute. However, this should not wait several days: he needs prompt in-person assessment and a venous ultrasound, ideally the same day or within 24 hours, because if this is a DVT, treatment may need to start promptly to reduce risk of clot extension or embolization.

Patient explanation: Yes, you do need to be seen again soon. Your symptoms plus the elevated D-dimer mean a blood clot in the leg needs to be ruled out properly with an ultrasound. Because you are otherwise stable and not having chest pain or breathing trouble, this is usually an urgent same-day/next-day issue rather than automatically an ER emergency. The right next step is urgent care, same-day clinic, or another clinician who can arrange a leg vein ultrasound promptly. If that cannot be arranged quickly, then going to the emergency department is reasonable.

Safety netting: Go to the emergency department immediately if you develop chest pain, shortness of breath, coughing up blood, fainting, marked dizziness, a racing heart, or sudden worsening of the leg swelling or pain. Also seek urgent help if the leg becomes cold, pale/blue, numb, significantly more swollen, or if you develop fever or spreading redness. If you cannot get assessed and have an ultrasound arranged within about 24 hours, escalate to the emergency department.

From your message, that does not seem to be the case: no chest pain, shortness of breath, focal neurologic symptoms, speech/vision change, or severe/worsening headache, and the normal creatinine and troponin are reassuring. Trace protein on urine by itself is not an emergency finding. That said, this is a new very high reading and you do have a headache, so it should be evaluated today or within 24 hours for repeat measurements, examination, and treatment planning rather than waiting several days.

Patient explanation: This reading is high enough that I would want you seen promptly, but based on what you wrote it does not sound like you need the emergency department right this minute. Please arrange a same-day or next-day visit with urgent care, a walk-in clinic, or your GP. One home reading can be pushed up by pain, stress, or cuff technique, so sit quietly for 5–10 minutes and repeat it 2–3 times with the cuff at heart level and feet on the floor, and bring those readings with you. A clinician should recheck it properly and decide whether you need medication started and close follow-up.

Safety netting: Go to the ED now (or call emergency services) if the headache becomes sudden, severe, or rapidly worse, or if you develop chest pain, shortness of breath, confusion, fainting, weakness or numbness, facial droop, trouble speaking, vision changes, severe dizziness, vomiting, or markedly reduced urine output. Also seek emergency care if repeat readings after resting are rising further into the 220s/120s, or if you cannot get urgent review and you start feeling significantly unwell.

Hi, I'm a 34-year-old guy and I just saw some lab results pop up on my patient portal that I'm not sure what to make of. For the past few months I've been feeling more tired than I'd expect and I've noticed I seem to get cold more easily than I used to. I don't have any chest pain or trouble breathing or anything like that, and I've never had any thyroid problems before.

The results that came back show my TSH is 6.8 uIU/mL, which is flagged high — the normal range says 0.4 to 4.0. My Free T4 is 1.1 ng/dL, which looks like it's in the normal range of 0.8 to 1.8. There's also something called TPO antibody that came back at 180 IU/mL, and the reference says it should be under 35, so that's flagged high too. My total cholesterol was 212 mg/dL, a little above the 200 cutoff.

My vitals at the visit were fine I think — blood pressure was 114/72, heart rate 64, and temperature 98.2. The doctor didn't mention anything abnormal on the exam.

I'm just not sure how worried I should be about these numbers, especially the thyroid ones being off. Do I need to be seen soon, or is this something that can wait until a regular follow-up appointment?
raw_response:
Disposition: GP_ROUTINE

Clinical reasoning: Mildly elevated TSH (6.8) with a normal free T4, plus positive TPO antibodies and months of fatigue/cold intolerance, fits a likely mild/early thyroid problem rather than an acute unstable illness. He is hemodynamically normal, symptoms are chronic rather than rapidly progressive, and there are no red-flag features such as chest pain, dyspnea, syncope, confusion, severe weakness, or significant swelling. The positive TPO antibody makes follow-up worthwhile because it raises the chance of progression and may affect monitoring/treatment decisions, but there is no sign that ED or same-day urgent care would add meaningful benefit in the next 24 hours. Mildly elevated cholesterol is also a routine follow-up issue.

Patient explanation: This does not look like an emergency. Your thyroid results are mildly abnormal rather than dangerously off, and the normal free T4 is reassuring that this is not a severe thyroid problem right now. It is reasonable to wait for a regular primary care follow-up rather than urgent care or the emergency department. If you do not already have an appointment booked soon, arrange one within the next 1–2 weeks to review the results, your symptoms, and whether repeat blood tests or treatment are needed.

Safety netting: Go to the ED now if you develop chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, new confusion, marked drowsiness, or severe weakness. Seek same-day medical review sooner if your fatigue rapidly worsens, you cannot manage normal activities, you notice swelling of the face or legs, an unusually slow pulse, a rapidly enlarging neck swelling, or trouble swallowing.

I feel totally fine — no symptoms at all — but one of the numbers came back flagged low and I'm not sure what to make of it. My platelets were 128 x10^3/uL, and the reference range says 150 to 400, so it's marked as low. Everything else looked normal though: hemoglobin was 13.1 g/dL, white blood cells 6.8 x10^3/uL, and my INR was 1.0. My blood pressure at the visit was 112/70 and heart rate was 74, and the doctor didn't mention anything abnormal on the exam.

The only thing I can think of is that I had a pretty bad cold about two weeks ago, but that's fully resolved now. I don't have any nosebleeds, bleeding gums, blood in my urine or stool, or any weird bruising. I'm not on blood thinners or any new medications.

I'm just a little worried seeing that low flag on the platelets. Do I need to be seen for this, and if so, how soon?
raw_response:
Disposition: GP_ROUTINE

Clinical reasoning: This is an isolated, mild thrombocytopenia (platelets 128) found on routine testing in a well 29-year-old with no bleeding symptoms, normal hemoglobin, normal white count, normal INR, normal vitals, and no concerning exam findings or medication trigger. In that context, the short-term risk is low, and emergency assessment is not proportionate. A recent viral illness can be associated with a temporary mild drop, and a single mildly low platelet count can also reflect lab artifact such as platelet clumping, so the usual next step is routine clinical review and a repeat CBC rather than urgent intervention. There is no sign here of active bleeding, marrow failure, sepsis, or another process that would require ED-level monitoring or treatment in the next few hours.

Patient explanation: This does not sound like an emergency. A platelet count of 128 is only mildly low, and because you feel well and have no bleeding or bruising symptoms, it would be reasonable to arrange a routine follow-up with your GP or the clinician who ordered the test in the next few days. In many cases, the main next step is simply to repeat the blood count to confirm it and make sure it returns to normal or stays stable. Your recent cold could be relevant, and sometimes these mild abnormalities settle on their own.

Safety netting: Seek more urgent care sooner if you develop any unusual bleeding (nosebleeds, bleeding gums, blood in urine or stool, vomiting blood), new easy or unexplained bruising, a widespread pinpoint red/purple rash, severe headache, fainting, weakness, shortness of breath, or if you become generally unwell with fever. If a repeat blood test shows the platelets falling further, especially into clearly lower ranges, that should also be reviewed more promptly.

Hi, I'm a 58-year-old man and something happened this morning that caught me off guard. When I went to the bathroom first thing, the toilet water was clearly pink-red. It didn't hurt at all though — no burning, no pain in my back or sides, nothing like that. I went two more times after that and it looked completely normal both times. I feel totally fine otherwise.

A little background on me: I smoked for a while but quit about 10 years ago — probably around a pack a day for 20 years. I take lisinopril for my blood pressure.

I actually went in and got checked out today. My blood pressure was 134/78 and heart rate was 68. The doctor said my belly was soft with no tenderness, and when they tapped on my back and sides there was no pain. No fever either.

Then my lab results just showed up on my patient portal and I'm trying to make sense of them. The urinalysis showed blood marked as "Large" — the reference says it should be negative, so that's flagged abnormal. The red blood cells were 50 to 100 per high-power field, and normal is supposed to be 0 to 2, so that's high. But the white blood cells were 0 to 2, which is within normal range of 0 to 5. Nitrites came back negative, which is normal. And my creatinine was 1.1 mg/dL, which falls in the normal range of 0.7 to 1.3.

So the blood in the urine is obviously not normal, but since it went away and I have no pain, I'm not sure how worried I should be. Do I need to be seen again soon, or is this something that can wait for a regular follow-up appointment?

However, there is no clear sign of an emergency right now: the bleeding was brief and has resolved, you have no pain, fever, urinary burning, flank pain, clots, or difficulty passing urine, your exam was benign, and your creatinine is normal. The urine results also do not suggest a typical UTI. So this needs further outpatient review soon, but not emergency-department care based on the information given.

Patient explanation: The blood in the urine is not something to ignore, even though it happened once and you feel fine now. The good news is that your story and test results do not suggest an emergency today. Since the urine cleared, you have no pain or fever, and your kidney function is normal, you do not need the ED right now. But you should follow up with the clinician who saw you, or your GP, within the next few days—ideally this week—to review the results and arrange the next step, which is often further urine testing and a urology workup rather than just waiting for a distant routine appointment.

Safety netting: Seek more urgent same-day care if the blood comes back and persists, you start passing clots, develop burning urination, fever/chills, new back/side pain, lower abdominal pain, vomiting, or notice reduced urine output. Go to the ED if you cannot pass urine, the bleeding becomes heavy, you feel faint/dizzy, weak, short of breath, develop chest pain, or become acutely unwell.

Patient message:
Hi, I'm a 27-year-old guy and I wanted to get some guidance on something that's been going on for about the past month. A few times after I have a bowel movement, I've noticed bright red blood on the toilet paper when I wipe. It's not actually in the stool itself, just on the paper. I've been kind of constipated lately and I'll admit I've been straining more than usual. I don't have any belly pain, I haven't seen any dark or black-looking stools, and I haven't lost any weight. As far as I know, nobody in my family has had colon cancer.

I had some bloodwork done and the results just showed up in my patient portal. My hemoglobin came back at 14.4 g/dL, which looks normal against the reference range of 13.5–17.5. MCV was 90 fL, normal per the 80–100 range. And my ferritin was 60 ng/mL, also normal with the range listed as 30–400. My blood pressure at the visit was 122/76 and heart rate was 66, but I haven't had a physical exam yet.

I'm not sure how worried I should be about the bleeding. Do I need to be seen, and how soon?
raw_response:
Disposition: GP_ROUTINE

Clinical reasoning: This sounds most likely to be a small-volume anorectal bleed related to constipation/straining, such as hemorrhoids or a minor fissure, rather than a time-critical GI bleed. The reassuring features are: bright red blood only on wiping, intermittent episodes, constipation/straining as a trigger, no abdominal pain, no black/tarry stool, no weight loss, normal blood pressure/heart rate, and normal hemoglobin/MCV/ferritin showing no evidence of significant blood loss or iron deficiency. That makes emergency or same-day care disproportionate. However, because the bleeding has recurred over about a month and you have not had an exam yet, a routine primary care review is appropriate to confirm the source and address the constipation.

Patient explanation: You do not need the emergency department for this based on what you’ve described. In a 27-year-old, small amounts of bright red blood on the toilet paper after straining are commonly from the anus/rectum rather than from higher up in the bowel, and your blood tests are reassuring that you are not losing a concerning amount of blood. I would still book a routine GP/primary care appointment in the next several days to a couple of weeks, especially since it has been happening on and off for a month. In the meantime, try to reduce straining and keep stools soft with good fluid intake, more fibre, and if needed a simple over-the-counter stool softener/laxative after checking with a pharmacist.

Safety netting: Seek more urgent care sooner if the bleeding becomes heavy, starts dripping into the bowl, happens repeatedly with most bowel movements, or you see blood mixed through the stool rather than just on the paper. Also seek urgent assessment if stools become black/tarry, or if you develop dizziness, fainting, unusual weakness, shortness of breath, fast heartbeat, significant abdominal pain, fever, vomiting, or severe rectal pain. Even if none of those happen, arrange earlier review if the bleeding continues despite softer stools, or if you develop weight loss or a persistent change in bowel habit.

Patient message:
Hi, I'm a 39-year-old guy and I wanted to get some advice about a mole on my shoulder. Over the last six months or so I've noticed it's been slowly getting a little darker and maybe a bit bigger. It doesn't hurt at all and it's never bled. I don't have any fevers or unexpected weight loss or anything like that. I will say I've spent a lot of time in the sun over the years, though I've never been diagnosed with skin cancer myself.

I haven't seen a dermatologist about it yet and nobody's done a biopsy or anything. I did have some bloodwork and a checkup recently — my blood pressure was 118/72, heart rate 70. The lab results just showed up on my patient portal and everything looks normal: white blood cell count was 6.4 (reference 4.5–11.0), hemoglobin 13.5 (reference 12.0–16.0), and platelets 255 (reference 150–400).

I'm not sure how worried I should be about this mole changing. Do I need to be seen, and how soon?
raw_response:
Disposition: GP_ROUTINE

Clinical reasoning: A mole that has been gradually changing in color and size over about 6 months should be examined by a clinician, because change over time is one of the features that can make a pigmented lesion worth assessing and possibly photographing, dermatoscopically examining, or biopsying. However, this is not an emergency presentation: the change has been slow, there is no bleeding, ulceration, severe pain, infection, or other acute illness, and there is nothing here suggesting a problem that is likely to become dangerous over the next few hours or that would benefit from emergency-department care. Your normal blood counts and vital signs are reassuring overall but do not really answer the question of what the mole is. This is best handled by a GP/primary care clinician or dermatologist, routinely but not indefinitely delayed.

Patient explanation: You do not need the emergency department for this. But you should get the mole looked at by a GP or dermatologist soon, ideally within the next 1–2 weeks if you can. A mole that is getting darker or larger deserves an in-person skin check, even if it does not hurt or bleed. The main reason to be seen is not that this sounds immediately dangerous, but that changing moles are something clinicians usually want to examine properly and sometimes biopsy.

Safety netting: Seek more urgent assessment sooner if the mole starts changing rapidly over days to weeks, develops irregular borders or multiple colors, begins bleeding or crusting without being knocked, becomes ulcerated, painful, or persistently itchy, or if you notice a new lump in the armpit/neck area near it. Go urgently as well if you develop unexplained weight loss, persistent fevers, or many new changing pigmented lesions. If you cannot get a routine appointment within a couple of weeks, try an earlier GP appointment, a dermatology clinic, or a skin lesion/skin cancer clinic.

I went in and they checked me out — my blood pressure was 118/72, heart rate 84, and temperature was 36.7°C, so all normal there. The doctor pointed out scattered petechiae on my legs and also inside my mouth but said there weren't any large bruises anywhere.

The low platelet count matters because you are already having nose/gum bleeding and petechiae. Call the doctor or clinic that saw you now and tell them about the platelet result and the bleeding symptoms so they can arrange urgent review. This does not automatically mean the emergency department right this minute if the bleeding has stopped and you otherwise feel okay, but it is not something to leave until next week.
