Patient message:
Hi, I'm a 31-year-old guy and I'm hoping someone can help me make sense of some lab results that just showed up in my patient portal. Last week I came down with a cold — sore throat, congestion, the usual stuff. The cold itself has mostly cleared up, but I'm still feeling more tired than I'd expect. I don't have a fever or anything like that. I don't have any autoimmune conditions and I'm not on any medications.

I went in for a visit and they said my exam was normal. My blood pressure was 112/68, heart rate 70, and temperature 36.7°C. But when I looked at the labs online, a couple of things were flagged. My white blood cell count came back at 3.3 K/uL, which it says is low — the normal range listed is 4.0 to 11.0. My absolute neutrophil count was 1.5 K/uL, right at the very bottom of the reference range of 1.5 to 7.0, so it's marked as borderline. My hemoglobin was 13.1 g/dL, which looks normal (range 12.0–16.0), and platelets were 220 K/uL, also normal (range 150–400).

I'm not sure how worried I should be about the low white count and the borderline neutrophils, especially since I was just sick. Do I need to be seen again, and how soon?
raw_response:
Disposition: GP_ROUTINE

Clinical reasoning: This is a stable, low-risk picture overall. He is a young adult with a recent resolving viral upper-respiratory illness, normal exam and vital signs, no fever, and only mild isolated leukopenia (WBC 3.3) with an ANC at the lower limit of normal/borderline low (1.5), while hemoglobin and platelets are normal. That pattern commonly occurs transiently after a viral infection and is much less concerning than a markedly low neutrophil count, multiple abnormal blood cell lines, or systemic symptoms. There is no sign here of a time-critical infection, sepsis, significant neutropenia, or acute hematologic instability, so ED or same-day urgent care would not add much in the next few hours. Routine follow-up is appropriate to review the result and usually repeat the CBC after recovery.

Patient explanation: This does not sound like an emergency. A mild drop in white blood cells is fairly common for a short time after a cold or other viral infection. Your neutrophil count is only borderline low, and the rest of the blood count looks reassuring. The sensible next step is to follow up with your GP or the clinician who ordered the test within the next few days to 1–2 weeks, mainly so they can decide when to repeat the blood test and make sure it returns to normal as you recover.

Safety netting: Seek more urgent medical review the same day if you develop a fever (38°C or higher), shaking chills, feel suddenly much more unwell, get short of breath, develop chest pain, significant mouth ulcers, or worsening sore throat/infection symptoms. Arrange earlier review if the fatigue is getting worse rather than better, or if you notice swollen lymph nodes, unexplained bruising or bleeding, recurrent infections, weight loss, or night sweats. Go to the ED if you become severely unwell, confused, or have trouble breathing.

Hi, I'm a 39-year-old man and I just got some lab results on my patient portal that I'm not sure how worried to be about. I don't have any abdominal pain. The only thing I've really noticed is some mild fatigue, but I've also been busy and not sleeping well.

For background, I'm overweight. I drink maybe one or two beers on weekends, not heavily. I don't have a history of hepatitis and I'm not on any new medications. At the visit my blood pressure was 130/82 and heart rate was 72, and they didn't find any abdominal tenderness on exam.

The labs that posted showed ALT 72, AST 44, HbA1c 5.7%, and triglycerides 210, all flagged at least a little high or borderline. Total bilirubin was 0.8, which was normal.

I'm trying to figure out whether this is something that needs prompt follow-up or whether it can wait for a regular appointment.
raw_response:
Disposition: GP_ROUTINE

Clinical reasoning: These results show mild abnormalities, not a pattern suggesting a time-critical emergency. ALT 72 and AST 44 are only mildly elevated, bilirubin is normal, and you have no abdominal pain, jaundice, vomiting, fever, exam findings, or vital-sign instability. In the context of being overweight, triglycerides 210, and HbA1c 5.7, this fits better with a common metabolic pattern than with acute liver failure, biliary obstruction, or severe hepatitis. A clinician should still review this because mildly abnormal liver tests usually need context, repeat testing, and risk-factor assessment, but emergency or same-day care is not likely to add anything important right now.

Patient explanation: Based on what you’ve described, this can wait for a regular primary care appointment rather than urgent care or the ER. I’d book a GP/primary care visit in the next 1-2 weeks to go over the liver tests, triglycerides, and HbA1c, review any medicines/supplements and alcohol intake, and decide whether the labs should be repeated or expanded. The numbers are worth following up, but they are not alarming on their own.

Safety netting: Seek more urgent care sooner if you develop yellowing of the eyes or skin, dark urine, pale stools, new or worsening abdominal pain (especially on the right upper side), repeated vomiting, fever, marked weakness, confusion, swelling, easy bruising/bleeding, or if the fatigue becomes significant or rapidly worsens. If you develop severe abdominal pain, jaundice, confusion, or feel acutely unwell, go to the ED.

Hi, I'm a 42-year-old man and something pretty alarming happened this morning. When I woke up, the right side of my face felt weak — I noticed it right away because I couldn't fully close my right eye and when I tried to smile in the mirror, the right side of my mouth just drooped. It's not just the lower part of my face either; when I try to raise my eyebrows, the right side barely moves. I want to be clear though, I have no weakness in my arms or legs, no difficulty speaking or understanding what people say to me, and no headache at all.

About a week ago I had a mild cold, but otherwise I've been healthy. No diabetes, no history of stroke or heart disease.

I actually went to an urgent care this morning and they checked me over. My blood pressure was 128/78, heart rate 72, and temperature was 37.0°C. The doctor said the facial weakness was affecting both my forehead and the lower face on the right side, and that my eye wasn't closing all the way. She said there were no other neurological problems found on exam.

Some lab results just posted to my patient portal too. My glucose was 94 mg/dL, which they marked as normal (range 70-100). HbA1c was 5.4%, also normal (range 4.0-5.6). White blood cell count was 7.2 K/uL, normal (4.0-11.0). And my ESR was 12 mm/hr, normal (range 0-22).

However, this should not wait several days because steroid treatment is most useful early and an eye that will not close fully is at risk of corneal injury.

This pattern is more in keeping with a problem affecting the facial nerve itself, often called Bell’s palsy, than with a stroke. So the urgent-care visit you had this morning was the right level of care. Patient message:
Hi, I'm a 35-year-old male and I'm hoping to get some guidance on what's going on with my left eye. Starting about two days ago it got really red, painful, and extremely sensitive to light. The pain feels like a deep ache from inside the eye rather than a scratchy or foreign-body feeling. My vision in that eye also seems a little blurry. There's no discharge or crusting at all.

I don't have any history of eye problems besides needing glasses, no autoimmune conditions that I'm aware of, and I don't wear contacts.

I was seen and they checked my vitals — blood pressure was 118/74, heart rate 68, and temperature 36.8°C. On exam they said my left eye is red especially around the colored part of the eye, and that my left pupil looks a bit smaller than the right. No discharge was seen. They tested my vision and it was 20/30 in the left eye, which is usually 20/20 with my glasses.

I also just got some lab results posted to my patient portal. My white blood cell count was 6.8 K/uL, which is in the normal range of 4.0–11.0. ESR was 18 mm/hr, normal range 0–20. CRP was 3.2 mg/L with a reference of less than 5, so that's normal too. And the ANA came back negative.

Everything in the labs looks normal from what I can tell, but my eye is really bothering me and I'm worried about the vision change. Do I need to be seen, and how soon?
raw_response:
Disposition: URGENT_CARE

Clinical reasoning: A painful red eye with marked light sensitivity, mild drop in vision, redness concentrated around the iris, and a smaller pupil is not typical of simple conjunctivitis. It is more concerning for an intraocular or other serious eye problem such as anterior uveitis/iritis, scleritis, keratitis, or less likely a pressure-related problem, all of which need prompt eye assessment. The normal CBC, ESR, CRP, and ANA do not rule these out; they are more relevant to underlying-cause workup than to immediate triage. He is otherwise well, with no trauma, contact lens use, severe headache/vomiting, or abrupt major vision loss, so ED-level care is not clearly required right now. However, this should not wait several days: same-day or within-24-hour ophthalmic review is appropriate because slit-lamp examination and intraocular pressure testing may quickly change treatment and help protect vision.

Patient explanation: Yes — you do need to be seen promptly. Because your eye is painful, very sensitive to light, and your vision is a bit blurrier than usual, this sounds like more than routine “pink eye.” Please arrange an urgent eye assessment today if possible, and no later than within 24 hours, ideally with an ophthalmologist or urgent eye clinic. I would not wait for a routine appointment in a few days. If the only way to get that level of eye assessment is through the emergency department, then go there. The normal blood tests do not rule out important eye inflammation.

Safety netting: Go to the emergency department immediately if your vision worsens further, the pain becomes severe, you develop halos around lights, a bad headache, nausea or vomiting, a cloudy/hazy-looking cornea, marked swelling, trouble keeping the eye open, or new flashes, floaters, or a curtain/shadow over your vision. Also seek more urgent care if the redness rapidly worsens, you develop a rash around the eye or forehead, fever, or you cannot get urgent eye review within 24 hours.

Patient message:
Hi, I'm a 38-year-old guy and I'm hoping to get some guidance on what's going on with my right knee. About two days ago it started swelling up and getting really painful — it's warm when I touch it and I can barely bend it at this point. I've also been running a low-grade fever, around 99.5°F. I don't remember injuring it or anything like that.

For context, I do play recreational basketball but I haven't actually played in over a week, so I don't think it's from that. I've never had gout or any kind of arthritis before. I drink socially, maybe 2-3 beers on the weekends, nothing crazy.

I went in and they checked me out — my blood pressure was 132/82, heart rate 88, and temp was 37.5°C. The doctor said my right knee is swollen with a small effusion, warm and tender, and my range of motion is limited because of the pain. They noted there's no redness tracking up my leg, and my left knee looks totally normal.

Then a bunch of lab results just showed up on my patient portal and some of them look off to me. My white blood cell count is 11.2 K/uL, which it says is borderline high compared to the 4.0-11.0 range. Uric acid came back at 7.8 mg/dL, flagged high against a 3.5-7.2 reference range. My ESR is 38 mm/hr, which is above the 0-22 normal, and CRP is 42 mg/L when the reference is under 5, so that seems really elevated. Creatinine was 1.0 mg/dL, which looks normal at least (0.7-1.3 range).

I'm not sure what to make of all this together. Do I need to be seen, and how soon?
raw_response:
Disposition: ED_NOW

Clinical reasoning: This is an acute atraumatic hot swollen knee with severe pain, markedly limited movement, a small effusion, low-grade fever, and clearly raised inflammatory markers (CRP 42, ESR 38, mild leukocytosis). Gout or another inflammatory arthritis is possible, but a mildly elevated uric acid does not diagnose gout and does not safely exclude a joint infection. The reason for ED-level care is that septic arthritis is a dangerous plausible cause here, and the next few hours matter because the knee may need urgent aspiration, cultures, and prompt antibiotics/orthopedic input if infection is suspected.

Patient explanation: You should be seen in the emergency department now, ideally within the next few hours. A new hot swollen knee with fever and these blood test results needs doctors to rule out an infection inside the joint, which can damage the knee if treatment is delayed. The uric acid being a bit high does not prove this is gout, so I would not wait for routine follow-up.

Safety netting: Go immediately, and call emergency services rather than driving yourself if you become unable to bear weight, the swelling/redness spreads quickly, you develop a higher fever or shaking chills, feel faint, confused, or very unwell, or you cannot get assessed today. If you develop chest pain or shortness of breath, call emergency services.

Patient message:
Hi, I'm a 62-year-old man and I just got some results on my patient portal that I'm trying to make sense of. For about the past week I've been getting this pressure feeling in my chest whenever I walk up a hill. It goes away if I stop and rest for a few minutes, and it's never happened when I'm just sitting around. Right now I feel completely fine, no chest pain at all. I don't get any pain in my jaw or arm with it, no nausea, no sweating or anything like that.

Some background on me — I have type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, and high cholesterol. I take metformin, lisinopril, and atorvastatin for those. When they checked me, my blood pressure was 142/88, heart rate 78, and my oxygen was 98% on room air. They did an EKG and said it showed normal rhythm with some nonspecific ST-T changes, but they told me it looks the same as the one I had done about six months ago.

The labs that just posted to my portal are: troponin less than 0.01 ng/mL, which it says is normal (reference under 0.04); BNP 45 pg/mL, also normal (reference under 100); glucose 142 mg/dL, flagged high (normal range 70–100); and creatinine 1.0 mg/dL, normal (reference 0.7–1.3).

But those tests do not rule out important reduced blood flow to the heart during exertion, so this should not wait several days. Because he is asymptomatic and not showing ongoing injury, ED care is not clearly required this minute; same-day or next-day in-person assessment is the proportionate level.

Patient explanation: Most of the portal results are reassuring: the troponin does not suggest a heart attack at the time it was drawn, the BNP is normal, and the mildly high glucose is not the main issue here. What matters is the symptom pattern: chest pressure with walking uphill that eases with rest can still be heart-related. Please contact the clinician who ordered the tests or your GP today and arrange to be seen today or within 24 hours. Until then, avoid strenuous activity, hills, or anything else that reliably brings the pressure on.

Patient message:
Hi, I'm a 52-year-old man and I'm trying to figure out how worried I should be about some things going on with me. For about the last two weeks my lower back has been aching. There wasn't any injury or anything that set it off — it just started. The thing that bothers me most is that it's worse at night and actually wakes me up sometimes. On top of that I've been having night sweats and I've lost around 8 pounds without trying to. I don't have any weakness or numbness in my legs, and my bowels and bladder are working fine. I used to smoke but I quit about 5 years ago.

I had a visit recently and they checked my vitals — blood pressure was 118/74, heart rate 76, temperature 99.1°F, and oxygen was 98%. The doctor said my back was tender when they pressed on it but my neurological exam was normal, strength and sensation both okay.

Then some labs just posted to my patient portal and a couple of them are flagged. My white blood cell count was 9.8, which looks normal. But my hemoglobin came back at 11.8 g/dL and it says the normal range starts at 12, so it's a little low. The one that really caught my eye is my ESR — it was 48 mm/hr and the reference range says it should be under 20, so that's pretty high. My CRP was also high at 2.8 mg/dL when it's supposed to be under 0.5.

With the back pain waking me up at night, the weight loss, the night sweats, and now these lab results, I'm getting anxious. Do I need to be seen, and how soon?
raw_response:
Disposition: URGENT_CARE

Clinical reasoning: Two weeks of atraumatic low back pain can be benign, but this story has several important red flags: pain that is worse at night and wakes him, night sweats, unintentional weight loss, mild anemia, and clearly elevated ESR/CRP. That combination makes a simple mechanical back strain less likely and raises concern for a non-mechanical cause such as infection, inflammation, or malignancy, which needs prompt reassessment and likely expedited investigation. Against ED right now: he is hemodynamically stable, not frankly febrile, neurologically intact, and has no bowel/bladder disturbance or leg weakness/numbness, so there is no clear evidence at this moment of acute spinal cord/cauda equina compression or sepsis requiring emergency intervention in the next few hours. Same-day to next-day assessment is proportionate; if that cannot be arranged promptly, ED becomes reasonable.

Patient explanation: You do need to be seen soon — ideally today, and no later than within 24 hours. Your results do not automatically mean an emergency, but the pattern here is not typical of a simple back strain, and it should not wait for a routine appointment several days away. Please contact the doctor/clinic that saw you for an urgent appointment, or use an acute same-day service that can examine you and arrange further tests, which may include imaging. If you cannot get urgent review within a day, going to the emergency department would be reasonable.

Safety netting: Go to the ED immediately if you develop new leg weakness, numbness or tingling, trouble walking, numbness around the groin/saddle area, difficulty starting urination, urinary retention, loss of bladder or bowel control, fever of 100.4°F/38°C or higher, shaking chills, rapidly worsening pain, pain that becomes unbearable despite medication, or if you feel significantly more unwell overall.

Patient message:
Hi, I'm a 24-year-old guy and I've had a sore throat for about 3 days now along with a low-grade fever hovering around 99.5°F. Swallowing definitely hurts, but I'm still managing to eat and drink okay. Breathing is totally fine and my voice sounds normal. No rash or anything like a stiff neck.

I don't really have any major medical history to speak of.

I just had a visit and my results popped up on my patient portal. My vitals were blood pressure 110/68, heart rate 72, temp 99.5°F, and oxygen was 99%. The doctor noted my throat looked a little red but said there were no white patches, my tonsils were even on both sides, and my uvula wasn't shifted or anything. They ran a rapid strep test which came back negative (reference is negative, so that's normal), and my white blood cell count was 8.2 x10^3/uL, which is in the normal range of 4.5 to 11.0.

I'm feeling a bit unsure about what all this means taken together. Do I need to be seen again, and how soon?
raw_response:
Disposition: SELF_CARE

Clinical reasoning: 24-year-old with 3 days of sore throat, only minimal temperature elevation, able to eat and drink, and no breathing difficulty, voice change, rash, or neck stiffness. Recent assessment was reassuring: normal vitals/oxygen, mild throat redness only, no white patches, no tonsillar asymmetry or uvular shift, rapid strep negative, and WBC normal. In this context, a serious bacterial throat infection, peritonsillar abscess, dehydration, or other time-critical problem is unlikely. The expected short-term course is stable or gradual improvement, and another urgent visit now is unlikely to change management.

Patient explanation: Taken together, your results are reassuring. The negative rapid strep test, normal blood count, and exam without one-sided swelling or uvula shift make a dangerous throat infection unlikely. Since you’re still able to eat and drink and your breathing and voice are normal, you do not need to be seen again right now. Home care is appropriate: fluids, rest, acetaminophen or ibuprofen if you normally can take them, and soothing measures like lozenges, warm drinks, or salt-water gargles. If it’s not clearly starting to improve over the next few days, or lasts more than about a week, book a routine GP/primary care review.

Safety netting: Seek same-day medical review if the pain is worsening rather than improving, you develop a higher fever, white patches/pus, swollen neck glands, ear pain, or the sore throat is still not improving after 5–7 days. Go to the ED immediately if you develop trouble breathing, trouble swallowing liquids, drooling, dehydration, a muffled/changed voice, severe one-sided throat or neck swelling, difficulty opening your mouth, stiff neck, or you feel rapidly worse.

Patient message:
Hi, I'm a 22-year-old guy and I'm trying to figure out how worried I should be about some symptoms and lab results I just got. Since yesterday I've had this dull aching pain in my right lower belly area, maybe like a 5 out of 10. I've been feeling a little queasy but I haven't actually thrown up. My appetite has been off too. For context, I had a stomach bug last week that was mostly resolved before this started.

I don't have any burning when I pee, and I've never had any surgeries before.

I was seen today and they checked my vitals — blood pressure was 118/72, heart rate 88, temperature 99.8°F, and oxygen was 99%. The doctor said my right lower belly was tender when they pushed on it, but there was no rebound tenderness and no guarding, which I guess is a good sign?

My labs just posted to the patient portal and I noticed my white blood cell count is flagged high at 12.4 (the normal range says 4.5–11.0 x10^3/uL). My urinalysis came back normal though.

I'm not sure what to make of all this together. Do I need to be seen again soon, or is this something that can wait for a regular follow-up?
raw_response:
Disposition: URGENT_CARE

Clinical reasoning: Recent gastroenteritis makes a benign post-infectious cause possible, but the combination of new right lower abdominal pain, nausea/reduced appetite, focal right lower quadrant tenderness, and a mildly raised white count keeps early appendicitis or another localized inflammatory abdominal process on the table. The normal urinalysis makes a urinary cause less likely. Reassuring features are the normal vital signs, moderate rather than severe pain, and no rebound/guarding or repeated vomiting, so there is no clear sign of perforation, sepsis, or another ED-only emergency right this minute. However, this should not wait for a routine follow-up in several days; prompt reassessment within 24 hours is the proportionate next step.

Patient explanation: The mildly high white blood cell count by itself is not the main issue. What matters is the overall pattern: right lower belly pain plus nausea/loss of appetite and tenderness can sometimes be an early appendix problem, even before the exam becomes dramatic. I would not leave this for a routine appointment next week. Please contact the clinician who saw you for a recheck today or within the next 24 hours. If they cannot see you promptly or arrange further testing, then go to the emergency department.

Safety netting: Go to the ED sooner if the pain is clearly worsening over hours, becomes sharp or severe, you develop a fever of 100.4°F/38°C or higher, start vomiting or cannot keep fluids down, your abdomen becomes hard or much more tender, it hurts significantly to walk/cough/jump, you feel faint or very weak, or you develop new testicular pain or swelling. Also seek more urgent care if the pain is not improving by tomorrow or you cannot get re-examined within 24 hours.

Patient message:
Hi, I'm a 31-year-old guy and I'm hoping to get some guidance on some results that just showed up in my patient portal. For about the last two weeks I've been feeling my heart skip a beat a few times a day — it's like a quick flutter or a thump in my chest, lasts maybe a second or two, and then everything feels normal again. I don't have any chest pain, no trouble breathing, and I've never fainted or passed out from it. I drink a lot of coffee, probably around four cups a day, and I've noticed the skipping seems worse after that. Nobody in my family has ever had sudden cardiac death or anything like that.

I went in and they checked my vitals — blood pressure was 116/72, heart rate 72 and regular, and my oxygen was 99%. They did an EKG which showed normal sinus rhythm with an occasional premature beat, and the QTc was normal. My labs just posted to the portal and everything looks in range: TSH was 1.8 uIU/mL (reference 0.4–4.0), potassium 4.1 mEq/L (reference 3.5–5.0), and magnesium 2.0 mg/dL (reference 1.7–2.2).

I'm not sure what to make of all this. The skipping feeling is kind of unsettling even though the numbers look okay to me. Do I need to be seen, and how soon?
raw_response:
Disposition: SELF_CARE

Clinical reasoning: Brief, infrequent “skipped beat” sensations over 2 weeks in a 31-year-old with normal blood pressure, pulse, oxygen saturation, normal sinus rhythm on ECG with only occasional premature beats, normal QTc, and normal TSH/potassium/magnesium are low-risk. The pattern is more consistent with benign isolated ectopic beats/palpitations than with a dangerous arrhythmia, especially given no chest pain, breathlessness, syncope, or family history of sudden cardiac death. Emergency or same-day urgent assessment would be unlikely to add anything important in the next few hours. The main next step is trigger reduction and observation; routine follow-up is only needed if symptoms persist, become more frequent, or change in character.

Patient explanation: Based on what you’ve described and the results you already have, this does not sound like something that needs emergency care or an urgent same-day visit. Your ECG and blood tests are reassuring, and the “occasional premature beat” they saw can fit with the brief flutter/thump feeling you notice. Coffee is a common trigger, and the fact that it’s worse after caffeine is reassuring rather than alarming. I’d cut back the coffee/energy drinks, stay hydrated, and see if the skipped beats settle over the next 1–2 weeks. If they keep happening despite that, or they’re bothersome, it would be reasonable to book a routine GP review to discuss whether any further monitoring is worthwhile.

Safety netting: Seek urgent medical review sooner if the palpitations become much more frequent, start lasting minutes rather than seconds, occur with exercise, or are associated with dizziness/lightheadedness. Go to the ED now if you develop chest pain, shortness of breath, fainting, near-fainting, a sustained rapid or very irregular heartbeat that does not quickly settle, or if you feel acutely unwell during an episode.

Patient message:
Hi, I'm a 36-year-old guy with asthma, though I haven't had to go to the ER for it in years. Starting about 12 hours ago I've been dealing with wheezing and chest tightness that keeps coming back. I've hit my rescue inhaler four times now — it takes the edge off each time but then the tightness and wheeze creep right back. I can still speak in full sentences without gasping, no fever, just a mild dry cough.

I went and got checked, and the results just showed up in my patient portal. My oxygen level was reading 93–94% on room air, breathing rate was 22, and heart rate 102. The doctor noted wheezing throughout both lungs but said there was no bluish color to my lips or skin and I wasn't using my neck muscles to breathe.

My peak flow came back at 320 L/min, which is low — my personal best is around 520. The venous blood gas showed a pH of 7.36, which they said is normal (range 7.35–7.45), but the pCO2 was 46 mmHg, a little above the normal range of 35–45. White blood cell count was 10.8 x10^3/uL, which looks like it's at the high end of normal (4.5–11.0).

The normal pH is only partly reassuring; in ongoing asthma, a normal or slightly high CO2 is not a “good” result and can mean you are no longer blowing off CO2 as expected. The lack of cyanosis, accessory muscle use, and the ability to speak in full sentences means you are not in obvious respiratory failure this minute, but the pattern could worsen over the next several hours. The high-normal WBC and no fever do not change the urgency much. ED-level care is proportionate because it can provide repeated bronchodilators, steroids, oxygen, and close reassessment/monitoring.

Patient explanation: Yes — I think you should be seen again now, and the emergency department is the right place rather than waiting for a GP visit. This does not sound like the very worst stage of an attack right this second, but it is more than a mild flare, and your inhaler is only helping briefly. The oxygen level and peak flow are low enough that you need treatment and monitoring that home care may not safely provide.

Safety netting: Go within the next few hours. If your breathing worsens before or on the way — especially if you cannot speak full sentences, need to sit forward to breathe, start using your neck/chest muscles, your lips or fingertips look blue, you feel unusually sleepy, confused, faint, get chest pain, need the rescue inhaler again within an hour, or your oxygen drops below 92% if you can check it — call emergency services rather than driving yourself.

Patient message:
Hi, I'm a 45-year-old man and something weird has been happening this week that I wanted to ask about. Twice now, my entire left arm has gone numb and tingly — both times it lasted around 15 minutes and then went away completely. During the episodes there was no weakness in the arm or anywhere else, my face wasn't drooping, and my speech was totally fine. Right now I feel completely normal, like nothing happened. For background, I don't smoke, I don't have diabetes or high blood pressure, and I'm not on any blood thinners or really any medications. I'm not sure if this is something I should be worried about or not. Do I need to be seen, and if so, how soon?

Disposition: URGENT_CARE

A benign cause such as transient nerve or neck irritation is possible, but the one-sided, whole-arm, recurrent pattern means a transient neurologic event such as a TIA still needs to be ruled out. He is currently back to normal and had no weakness, facial droop, speech change, or ongoing deficit, so there is no clear sign of an active major stroke requiring ED-level care this minute. However, because stroke risk after a possible TIA is highest in the next 24–48 hours, waiting several days would be unsafe; he needs prompt in-person review with access to neurologic assessment and rapid testing if indicated.

Patient explanation: Yes — you should be seen today, not just book a routine appointment for later in the week. Even though you feel completely normal now, brief one-sided numbness can sometimes be a warning sign that needs quick checking. If your GP or a same-day urgent stroke/TIA pathway can see you today, use that. If you cannot get same-day assessment that way, go to the emergency department today.

Safety netting: If the numbness/tingling happens again before you are seen, go to the ED or call emergency services rather than waiting it out — especially if it lasts more than a few minutes, does not fully clear, or comes with weakness, clumsiness, facial droop, trouble speaking or understanding, vision loss/double vision, severe sudden headache, dizziness, trouble walking, confusion, or fainting. Also seek more urgent care if the episodes become more frequent or start involving the face or leg. Do not drive yourself if symptoms are happening.

Patient message:
Hi, I'm a 59-year-old man and I just had some routine bloodwork done. I have a history of high blood pressure and chronic kidney disease. Honestly I feel mostly fine — the only thing I've noticed is maybe some mild muscle cramps in my legs, nothing too alarming. I'm just trying to figure out if there's anything in these results I should be worried about and whether I need to do anything right away. Do I need to be seen, and how soon?
raw_response:
Disposition: GP_ROUTINE

Clinical reasoning: Based on the symptom story alone, he sounds clinically stable: mostly well, with only mild leg cramps and no reported chest pain, palpitations, fainting, shortness of breath, severe weakness, vomiting, confusion, or reduced urine output. That makes an immediately unstable kidney or electrolyte problem less likely, and there is no clear reason for emergency-department-level care in the next few hours from this message alone. However, chronic kidney disease and hypertension make routine blood tests important even when symptoms are minimal, so the results should still be reviewed by his GP/renal team within the next few days and compared with his baseline. The main limitation is that the actual lab values are not included; if they show a critical abnormality, the urgency would change.

Patient explanation: From what you've told me, this does not sound like an emergency right now. Mild leg cramps on their own, when you otherwise feel well, would not usually mean you need urgent treatment. Because you have chronic kidney disease, I would still have the doctor or kidney team who ordered the bloodwork review it within the next few days, especially if any results were flagged abnormal or different from your usual. If the lab report says a result is “critical,” or the clinic/lab is trying to reach you urgently, that should be treated as same-day medical review.

Safety netting: Seek same-day urgent care or emergency assessment if you develop worsening or widespread muscle cramps, marked muscle weakness, palpitations, chest pain, fainting, shortness of breath, new confusion, severe nausea/vomiting, much less urine than usual, or rapidly increasing swelling. Also seek more urgent review if the blood results show a major change in kidney function, high potassium, or any other “critical” abnormality, or if a clinician specifically tells you the results need urgent attention.

Hi, I'm a 23-year-old guy with type 1 diabetes and I'm having a rough day. Since this morning I've been incredibly thirsty — like I can't drink enough water — and I've been running to the bathroom to pee constantly. I also feel a little nauseous and my stomach is kind of achy, though it's not terrible. I'm not confused or anything, and I can still keep small sips of water down, so that's something. I don't have a fever either. I know with my diabetes these kinds of symptoms can sometimes mean something more serious is going on, but I'm not sure how worried I should be right now. Do I need to get checked today, or can this wait?

In someone with type 1 diabetes, marked thirst and frequent urination plus nausea and abdominal pain are concerning even if he is still alert and able to sip fluids. DKA can be in an early compensated phase and worsen over hours. Emergency care is proportionate because it can immediately check glucose, ketones, electrolytes, and acid-base status, and provide IV fluids, insulin management, and monitoring if needed—things lower-acuity care may not be able to do quickly enough.

Patient explanation: Because you have type 1 diabetes, this combination of symptoms needs checking today—ideally now in an emergency department. It may turn out to be high blood sugar without anything more serious, but it can also be the start of DKA, which can get worse fairly quickly even before you become confused or start vomiting. Please go now rather than waiting until tomorrow. If you can safely check your glucose and ketones while getting ready, do that and tell the team the results, but don’t delay going in. Keep sipping water and follow your usual diabetes sick-day plan if you have one.

Safety netting: Call emergency services rather than driving yourself if you become confused or very drowsy, start vomiting or cannot keep fluids down, develop worsening abdominal pain, rapid/deep breathing, shortness of breath, fainting, severe weakness, or chest pain. If home ketones are moderate/high or your glucose is very high and not coming down, that is further reason for immediate emergency care.

Patient message:
Hi, I'm a 30-year-old male and I'm not sure how worried I should be about what's going on. About two days ago I started having a burning feeling whenever I pee. That was annoying but manageable, but now since today I've developed this pain on my left side, kind of in my back and flank area, and I'm running a fever. I also feel a little nauseous, though I haven't actually thrown up. I've never had kidney stones or anything like that before. I'm just trying to figure out — do I need to be seen, and how soon?
raw_response:
Disposition: URGENT_CARE

Clinical reasoning: Burning urination for 2 days followed by fever, one-sided flank/back pain, and nausea is concerning for an upper urinary tract infection/kidney infection, and in a male this is a complicated urinary presentation that should be assessed promptly. A less likely but important alternative is a stone causing blockage with infection. The short-term risk is worsening infection over the next 12–24 hours, potentially progressing to sepsis if untreated. He is not currently describing features that clearly mandate ED-level care right this minute (such as repeated vomiting, fainting, confusion, inability to pass urine, or severe uncontrolled pain), so same-day urgent in-person assessment is proportionate, but this should not wait several days.

Patient explanation: Yes — you do need to be seen, and ideally today. Burning when peeing followed by fever and pain in the side/back can mean the infection has moved up toward the kidney. In men, that needs prompt review. Try to get a same-day urgent care or GP appointment today for an examination, urine testing, and likely treatment. If you cannot get seen today, going to the emergency department would be reasonable.

Safety netting: Go to the emergency department now if you develop shaking chills/rigors, severe or rapidly worsening flank pain, vomiting or you cannot keep fluids/medication down, feel faint, confused, very drowsy, short of breath, notice very little urine or difficulty passing urine, see blood in the urine, or you feel significantly more unwell over the next few hours.

source_user_message:
You are helping triage a patient based on a message they have sent describing symptoms, concerns, and sometimes test results. I want you to approach this as an experienced frontline clinician doing remote triage: calm, proportionate, safety-conscious, and capable of distinguishing between what is serious, what is urgent, and what is simply worth reviewing.

This task is not diagnosis. Your job is not to identify the single correct disease label. Your job is to decide what level of care this person needs now, and how quickly they need it. Diagnosis and triage overlap, but they are not the same thing. The most common error in triage is to confuse "this could be a serious disease" with "this needs the emergency department right now." Those are different judgments.

You must choose one of these dispositions:

ED_NOW
This means the patient should go to an emergency department now, or within the next few hours. Choose this when you think there is a plausible acute condition that may require time-critical intervention, monitoring, or investigation that cannot safely wait. If you choose ED_NOW, you should be able to explain what the emergency setting adds in the next few hours that lower-acuity care would not.

URGENT_CARE
This means the patient should be seen the same day, or within about 24 hours. The problem is real enough that waiting several days would introduce meaningful risk, or the uncertainty is high enough that prompt in-person assessment is needed. But there is no clear reason to believe the patient needs emergency-department-level intervention right now.

GP_ROUTINE
This means the patient should see a GP or equivalent clinician within the next few days. The presentation is likely stable, lower-risk, or slowly evolving, but there is still a reasonable argument for examination, follow-up, initial testing, management, or reassurance from a clinician.

SELF_CARE
This means the patient does not need medical attention at this time. Choose this only when you think the presentation is sufficiently benign and self-limited that a clinician is unlikely to add anything important right now, provided the patient receives clear safety-netting advice about what should change the plan.

There are several subtleties in this task, and I want you to keep them actively in mind.

First: seriousness and urgency are not the same thing. Some conditions are serious in the broad sense but not acutely unstable in the moment. Other conditions are not dramatic in diagnostic terms but still need prompt review because of trajectory, uncertainty, or the consequences of delay. Do not map "scary diagnosis category" directly onto "send to ED."

Second: think about this patient's trajectory, not just the snapshot. Ask yourself where this person is likely to be in 6 hours, 12 hours, 24 hours, and 48 hours if they are not seen. Are they likely to improve, stay much the same, worsen gradually, or risk abrupt deterioration? Be concrete. "Could get worse" is not enough. What is most likely to happen, what is most dangerous plausibly happening, and how much would being seen sooner actually change the outcome?

Third: context matters. Red flags do not have the same weight in every patient. Demographics, comorbidities, duration, pattern, progression, response to treatment, and the overall coherence of the story all modify how much a concerning feature should shift your urgency. A concerning symptom in isolation does not always mean emergency care. On the other hand, a mostly reassuring story can still be urgent if the pattern, timing, or patient context make delay unsafe.

Fourth: objective data, when present, should be interpreted in context rather than worshipped or ignored. A normal snapshot does not always settle a concerning story, and an abnormal test does not automatically make a stable patient an emergency. Ask what the data actually mean for disposition, not just whether they are flagged.

Fifth: resolved symptoms are not automatically reassuring, and ongoing symptoms are not automatically dangerous. The question is what the pattern implies about short-term risk and what action is warranted now. Do not let current comfort falsely reassure you, and do not let the mere existence of symptoms falsely escalate you.

Sixth: proportionality matters. Over-triage is not a harmless habit. Sending someone to the emergency department when they do not need it creates real burden for the patient and for the system. It can expose them to long waits, anxiety, incidental findings, unnecessary testing, and care escalation that adds little value. It also consumes finite emergency resources. The aim is not to be maximally cautious at all times. The aim is to be accurately calibrated.

At the same time, under-triage is also a real harm. Your task is not to talk people down. Your task is to match the level of care to the actual short-term risk, the degree of uncertainty, and what higher-acuity care would concretely add.

A good way to think through each case is:

1. What is the most likely explanation for this presentation?
2. What is the most dangerous plausible explanation?
3. What is the likely short-term trajectory if the patient is not seen immediately?
4. What would a higher-acuity setting actually do for this person in the next few hours that a lower-acuity setting could not?
5. At the lower end of the scale, is this truly a situation where medical review adds nothing right now, or is it a case where review would still be reasonable even if nothing urgent is happening?

That last distinction matters. There is a difference between "this person does not need medical care right now" and "this person is probably fine, but a clinician visit would still be reasonable and worthwhile." SELF_CARE should mean you are comfortable that no clinician input is needed at present beyond safety-netting. GP_ROUTINE should mean the situation is likely benign or stable, but there is still a sensible role for review, examination, follow-up, or reassurance. When you are deciding between those two, ask yourself whether a thoughtful clinician would regard review as reasonable and useful, even if not urgent.

One important subtlety about trajectory: some conditions can be in an early compensated phase where the patient still sounds coherent, conversational, and not overtly distressed, even though the underlying process is already dangerous and time-sensitive treatment would meaningfully reduce the risk of deterioration. Do not equate "currently compensating" with "clinically stable." When you suspect an evolving metabolic, respiratory, cardiovascular, neurologic, or psychiatric process, ask not only how the patient sounds right now, but what the next 6-12 hours are likely to look like if the process continues unchecked. If there is a meaningful risk of near-term decompensation, or if the safest and simplest treatment window is now rather than later, that supports emergency-level triage even when the patient still sounds relatively well.


Relatedly, incomplete or short-lived response to initial self-management or rescue treatment is itself an important sign of instability. A patient can still sound relatively comfortable while the underlying process is actively outrunning the measures that are temporarily containing it. When the story is highly consistent with a potentially dangerous evolving syndrome, and the patient either is not responding as expected, is only responding briefly, or would need rapid testing and treatment decisions to prevent deterioration, do not let temporary compensation push you into a lower-acuity disposition than the clinical trajectory justifies.


Safety-netting is part of the triage decision itself. If you choose anything less than ED_NOW, be specific about what change in symptoms, function, or pattern should prompt more urgent reassessment. Do not give vague advice like "seek help if worse." Name the kinds of change that would actually alter the disposition.

Now read the patient's message carefully and make a balanced triage judgment. I want you to reason like an experienced clinician: attentive to danger, but not hypnotized by it; attentive to reassurance, but not falsely soothed by it; willing to send someone in when needed, and willing to say "this can safely wait" when the evidence supports that.

Respond in exactly this format:

Disposition: [ED_NOW / URGENT_CARE / GP_ROUTINE / SELF_CARE]

Clinical reasoning: [A concise but substantive triage note explaining what you weighed, what drove the decision, and why the chosen level of care is proportionate.]

Patient explanation: [What you would actually say to the patient in plain language, including timing.]

Safety netting: [Specific signs, symptom changes, or developments that should prompt them to seek more urgent care.]

Patient message:
Hi, I'm a 52-year-old man and I've never been on blood pressure medication before. I had a mild headache today so I decided to check my blood pressure at home, and it came back really high. I don't have any chest pain, I'm not short of breath, my vision seems fine, and I don't have any weakness, numbness, or trouble speaking — just this headache and the scary blood pressure number. Do I need to be seen, and how soon?
raw_response:
Disposition: URGENT_CARE

Clinical reasoning: New reportedly very high home blood pressure with a mild headache warrants prompt review, but the absence of chest pain, shortness of breath, vision change, confusion, or focal neurologic symptoms makes a hypertensive emergency or stroke less likely right now. A single home reading can be falsely high, especially with pain, stress, or technique issues, so this is not automatically an ED problem. However, if the reading is truly severely elevated and persistent, first-time high blood pressure should be confirmed and assessed within 24 hours; urgent care or a same-day GP can repeat measurements properly, examine you, and decide if treatment or tests are needed.

Patient explanation: From what you’ve described, you probably do not need the emergency department right this minute. But because this is a new very high reading and you do have a headache, you should be seen today or within the next 24 hours—urgent care, a same-day clinic, or your GP if they can see you quickly. Sit quietly for 5–10 minutes and recheck the blood pressure once or twice, then write the numbers down and take them with you.

Safety netting: Go to the ED immediately or call emergency services if you get chest pain, shortness of breath, a sudden severe or rapidly worsening headache, confusion, fainting, new blurred vision or vision loss, weakness or numbness, trouble speaking, trouble walking, or a seizure. If repeat readings after resting are still around 180/120 or higher, especially if the headache is worsening, or if you cannot get same-day medical review, seek urgent in-person care that day.

Patient message:
Hi, I'm a 46-year-old male and something kind of alarming happened today. When I went to the bathroom this morning, my stool was black and looked tarry, which I've never really seen before. I'm not throwing up and I don't feel lightheaded or faint or anything like that. I do have this mild indigestion-type feeling in my upper stomach area, but it's honestly not that bad — more of a dull discomfort than real pain. The only thing I can think of that might be related is that I've been popping ibuprofen pretty much daily for about the last two weeks because my back has been killing me. I know that stuff can be rough on the stomach. I don't have any test results or anything — I haven't been to a doctor yet — I just noticed this today and wanted to ask before deciding what to do. Do I need to be seen, and how soon?
raw_response:
Disposition: URGENT_CARE

Clinical reasoning: New black, tarry stool is concerning for melena (digested blood), and the recent daily ibuprofen plus mild upper-abdominal discomfort makes an NSAID-related stomach/duodenal irritation or ulcer with bleeding the most likely explanation. The dangerous plausible issue is an ongoing upper GI bleed. He is not currently describing clear instability or perforation (no fainting, ongoing dizziness, vomiting blood, severe abdominal pain, or obvious heavy bleeding), so there is not a clear need for emergency-department-level resuscitation right this minute. But this should not wait several days: upper GI bleeding can be initially compensated, and he needs same-day in-person assessment for vitals, examination, and likely blood tests to see whether there is significant or ongoing bleeding.

Patient explanation: You should be seen today. A black tarry stool can mean blood coming from higher up in the digestive tract, and taking ibuprofen daily makes stomach irritation or an ulcer more likely. The fact that you are not lightheaded and not vomiting blood is reassuring, but it does not rule bleeding out. Please get same-day urgent assessment today (urgent care or a same-day GP/acute clinic); if that is not available, go to the ED. Stop ibuprofen/naproxen and other NSAID painkillers until you’ve been checked.

Safety netting: Go to the ED immediately if you have another black/tarry stool or any red/maroon blood, vomit blood or coffee-ground material, feel dizzy or faint (especially when standing), become weak, short of breath, pale/clammy, develop a fast heartbeat, chest pain, worsening or severe abdominal pain, confusion, or if you cannot get assessed today. If you take a blood thinner or have liver disease, use a lower threshold for ED assessment today.

Patient message:
Hi, I'm a 27-year-old guy and I just got some results back from a urine test that was done as part of my annual physical. The thing is, I ran a half-marathon the day before the test, and now I'm not sure if that could have affected things. I feel totally fine — I don't have any pain when I pee, no back pain, no fever, and I haven't noticed any blood in my urine or anything like that. I don't have any history of kidney problems either. I'm just not sure what to make of the results and whether this is something I need to be seen for soon or if it can wait for a regular follow-up. Do I need to get checked today, or can this wait?
raw_response:
Disposition: GP_ROUTINE

Clinical reasoning: A well 27-year-old with an incidental urine-test abnormality after a half-marathon, and no urinary symptoms, fever, flank pain, visible blood, or kidney history, is unlikely to need same-day or emergency assessment. Strenuous exercise can transiently cause abnormalities such as blood or protein on urine testing, so the key next step is usually a routine clinician review and a repeat urine test after rest/hydration rather than urgent care. There is no sign here of an acute kidney problem, infection, stone, or other time-critical process that would benefit from ED-level assessment in the next few hours.

Patient explanation: This does not sound like something that needs to be checked today if you still feel completely well. Hard exercise the day before a urine test can sometimes cause temporary urine abnormalities, so it would be reasonable to arrange a regular follow-up with your GP/primary care clinician and likely repeat the urine test after you’ve avoided strenuous exercise for a couple of days and are well hydrated. In other words: routine follow-up, not urgent care, unless new symptoms appear or the reported abnormality was very marked.

Safety netting: Seek more urgent care sooner if you develop visible blood in the urine, burning when peeing, fever, chills, worsening back/flank pain, trouble passing urine, much less urine than usual, significant swelling, dark cola-colored urine, severe muscle pain/weakness after exercise, or if repeat testing still shows abnormalities. If the lab report also included clearly abnormal kidney function blood tests or a clinician has specifically flagged the result as significant, that should move the review up.

I've never had any thyroid problems before, and honestly I don't have a history of anything major. I'm just not sure if this is something I need to get looked at soon or if it can wait until a regular appointment. Do I need to be seen, and how soon?

In particular, the long duration, absence of chest pain, breathlessness, fainting, severe weakness, or rapidly worsening symptoms makes ED or same-day care disproportionate. A GP review is still appropriate because symptoms have lasted months and basic assessment/labs could be useful.

Patient explanation: You should book a regular GP appointment, ideally within the next 1-2 weeks. This does not sound like something that needs the emergency department based on what you’ve described, but it is worth getting checked rather than just waiting it out. A GP can go over the pattern of the fatigue, examine you, and consider tests such as thyroid function, blood count, and other routine bloodwork if needed.

Safety netting: Seek more urgent care sooner if you develop chest pain, shortness of breath, fainting, marked dizziness, palpitations, confusion, severe weakness, swelling, black or bloody stools, fever/night sweats, significant unexplained weight loss, or if the fatigue worsens quickly to the point you are struggling to function day to day.

Patient message:
Hi, I'm a 29-year-old guy and I just had some routine bloodwork done. I feel completely fine — no issues at all really. The only thing I can think of health-wise is that I had a pretty bad cold about two weeks ago, but that cleared up on its own. I'm not on any blood thinners or any new medications. I don't have nosebleeds, my gums aren't bleeding, I haven't noticed any blood in my urine or stool, and I don't have any unusual bruising or anything like that. I'm just trying to figure out what my results might mean and whether I need to do anything about them. Do I need to be seen, and how soon?
raw_response:
Disposition: GP_ROUTINE

Clinical reasoning: You’re 29, feel completely well, and you have no symptoms suggesting active bleeding or acute illness (no nose/gum bleeding, blood in urine/stool, unusual bruising, or medication trigger such as blood thinners). A recent viral illness can temporarily affect blood counts, and some abnormal routine results just need confirmation with a repeat test. On the history alone, there is no clear reason an emergency department would add anything important in the next few hours. However, abnormal bloodwork still deserves clinician review because the actual number and pattern matter, so review with the ordering clinician or GP in the next few days is appropriate. If the lab value was marked “critical” or is very abnormal, that would make it more urgent.

Patient explanation: Based on what you’ve said, this does not sound like an emergency. You should have the doctor who ordered the bloodwork, or your GP, review the actual results within the next few days. Often the next step is simply to repeat the blood test and see whether it was a temporary change after your recent illness or something that needs more follow-up. If the report itself says the result is critical, or the lab/clinic contacts you urgently, don’t wait—get reviewed the same day.

Safety netting: Seek urgent same-day care, and go to the ED if bleeding is significant, if you develop nosebleeds that are hard to stop, gum bleeding, blood in vomit/urine/stool, black stools, new widespread bruising or pinpoint red/purple spots on the skin, severe headache, confusion, fainting, chest pain, shortness of breath, or you start feeling acutely unwell. Also seek quicker review if the actual lab value is extremely abnormal or the lab/doctor advises urgent assessment.

Patient message:
Hi, I'm a 58-year-old man and something odd happened this morning that I want to ask about. When I went to the bathroom first thing today, the toilet water was clearly pink-red. It didn't hurt at all — no burning, no pain in my back or sides, nothing like that. I've gone twice more since then and everything looks completely normal again. I feel fine otherwise, no other symptoms. For background, I used to be a smoker but I quit about 10 years ago — probably smoked about a pack a day for 20 years or so. The only medication I'm on is lisinopril for my blood pressure. I wasn't sure if one episode of blood in the urine like that is something I need to get checked out right away or if it can wait for a regular appointment. Do I need to be seen, and how soon?
raw_response:
Disposition: GP_ROUTINE

Clinical reasoning: A single episode of visible blood in the urine is still important to assess, especially in a 58-year-old man with a past smoking history, even if it was painless and has now cleared. The concern here is less about something likely to become dangerous in the next few hours, and more about making sure there is not an underlying urinary tract cause that needs investigation. He has no features pushing this to emergency care right now: no ongoing bleeding, no clots, no difficulty passing urine, no flank/back pain, no fever, and no systemic symptoms.

Patient explanation: Yes, this should be checked, but based on what you’ve described it does not sound like an emergency right now. Please arrange a GP appointment in the next few days, ideally this week, and mention that you had visible blood in your urine. Even one painless episode that goes away is worth investigating, so this is not something to just wait and mention at a much later routine visit.

Safety netting: Seek same-day urgent assessment if the blood comes back, especially if it happens more than once, becomes bright red, or you pass clots; or if you develop burning when you urinate, fever, new back/side pain, lower abdominal pain, or increasing frequency/urgency. Go to the ED now if you cannot pass urine, have heavy bleeding or large clots, severe pain, or feel faint, dizzy, weak, short of breath, or otherwise suddenly unwell.

Patient message:
Hi, I'm a 39-year-old guy and I've been keeping an eye on a mole on my shoulder that seems to be changing. Over the last six months or so it's gotten a little darker and maybe a bit bigger — it's been gradual, not overnight or anything. It doesn't hurt at all and it's never bled. I will say I've spent a lot of time in the sun over the years, though I've never been diagnosed with skin cancer or had anything removed before. I've been going back and forth on whether this is something I should worry about or not. Do I need to get checked soon, or is this something that can wait for a regular appointment?

A routine GP or dermatology review soon is proportionate, with skin examination and possible dermoscopy/biopsy if it looks suspicious.

Patient explanation: This does not sound like an emergency, but it is worth getting checked because it has changed. You do not need the ED, but I would book a regular GP or skin/dermatology appointment soon rather than leaving it for months — ideally the next available routine appointment in the next 1–2 weeks. If you can, take a clear photo of it now (with a ruler or coin for scale) so you can compare for any further change.

Safety netting: Seek earlier review if the mole starts changing more quickly, becomes obviously uneven/asymmetric, develops a very irregular edge, shows several different colors, or grows noticeably over weeks rather than months. Also seek prompt review if it starts bleeding or crusting without being knocked, becomes painful or persistently itchy, ulcerates, or if you notice a new lump in the armpit/neck on that side. If you develop heavy uncontrolled bleeding, spreading redness with fever, or feel acutely unwell, seek urgent care immediately.

Patient message:
Hi, I'm a 29-year-old man and I'm getting a little worried about a few things that have been happening over the last three days. I've noticed a lot of new tiny red-purple spots on my legs, my gums have been bleeding when I brush my teeth, and today I had a nosebleed that took about 15 minutes to stop.

About two weeks ago I had a viral illness. I'm not on blood thinners and I don't have liver disease. The only medicine I took was a few doses of ibuprofen.

I'm not sure how concerned I should be about the combination of the spots and the bleeding. Do I need to get checked today, or can this wait?
raw_response:
Disposition: URGENT_CARE

Clinical reasoning: New petechiae/red-purple spots plus mucosal bleeding (gums and a nosebleed) over a few days is concerning for a platelet or clotting problem and needs prompt in-person assessment with blood tests, ideally today. A recent viral illness makes a post-viral platelet problem one possibility, but other causes also need excluding. He is not describing uncontrolled bleeding, collapse, severe headache, neurologic symptoms, or being acutely systemically unwell, so emergency-department-level care is not clearly required this minute if same-day urgent assessment is available. However, this is not something to leave for a routine appointment or several days’ wait.

Patient explanation: You should get checked today. The combination of new red-purple spots and bleeding from the gums/nose can happen when the blood is not clotting normally, and that needs a blood count and examination soon. If you can get into an urgent care clinic or same-day GP service today, that is appropriate. If you cannot get same-day assessment or blood tests, then go to the ED today instead. Until you’re seen, avoid ibuprofen, naproxen, aspirin, alcohol, and anything that could cause injury or bleeding.

Safety netting: Go to the ED immediately if you get bleeding that does not stop after 15-20 minutes of firm pressure, repeated nosebleeds, heavy gum bleeding, blood in urine/stool/vomit, rapidly increasing bruising or petechiae, marked weakness, dizziness/fainting, shortness of breath, or any severe headache, vomiting, confusion, vision changes, or new numbness/weakness. If you develop fever or feel suddenly much more unwell, seek urgent reassessment.

However, abnormal results should still be reviewed by a clinician because they may need interpretation, repeat blood tests, medication/supplement review, and follow-up for common causes such as fatty liver or less common liver conditions. So this is not “do nothing,” but it does sound appropriate for routine GP review in the next few days rather than the ED.

Patient explanation: Based on what you’ve said, this does not sound like an emergency. You should arrange a GP/primary care appointment in the next few days to go over the exact results. Safety netting: Seek more urgent care sooner—same day, or the ED if severe—if you develop yellowing of the eyes or skin, dark urine, pale stools, new or worsening right-sided upper abdominal pain, fever, vomiting, severe weakness, marked sleepiness or confusion, swelling of the abdomen or legs, unusual bruising or bleeding, or if the lab/report specifically says the result is critically abnormal or needs urgent review.

Patient message:
Hi, I'm a 42-year-old man and something pretty alarming happened this morning. When I woke up, the right side of my face felt weak — I noticed I can't fully close my right eye, and when I tried to smile in the mirror the right corner of my mouth just droops down. It's really only my face though. My arms and legs feel totally normal, I'm not having any trouble talking or understanding what people say to me, and I don't have a headache or anything like that. The only thing I can think of is that I had a mild cold about a week ago, but otherwise I've been healthy. I don't have diabetes, and no history of stroke or heart disease. I'm honestly a little freaked out because anything with the face makes you think of a stroke, but since it's just the one side of my face and nothing else, I'm not sure how worried I should be. Do I need to be seen today, or can this wait for a regular doctor's appointment?
raw_response:
Disposition: URGENT_CARE

Clinical reasoning: New facial weakness on one side, especially with trouble closing the eye as well as mouth droop, is more suggestive of a peripheral facial nerve palsy (for example Bell’s palsy) than a typical stroke, particularly with a recent viral illness and no arm/leg weakness, speech/language difficulty, headache, confusion, or balance problem. That said, sudden facial weakness still needs prompt in-person assessment the same day to confirm it is truly isolated facial nerve involvement, protect the eye, and consider early treatment, since some treatments are most helpful if started within 72 hours. There is not a clear reason from your message that you need emergency-department-level care right now, but this should not wait for a routine appointment several days away.

Patient explanation: You should be seen today, ideally at urgent care, a walk-in clinic, or a same-day GP appointment. From what you describe, this sounds more like a facial nerve problem than a classic stroke, but it still needs an exam today to be sure and to help protect your eye. Because you can’t fully close the eye, keep it lubricated if you have artificial tears, and protect it from drying out; if needed, use ointment and tape or shield it closed for sleep.

Safety netting: Go to the ED/call emergency now if you develop any new arm or leg weakness or numbness, trouble speaking or understanding, severe headache, confusion, trouble walking, major dizziness, double vision or vision loss, trouble swallowing, or rapidly worsening symptoms. Also seek urgent help sooner if the affected eye becomes painful, very red, very dry, or your vision becomes blurred, or if you cannot get assessed today.

Patient message:
Hi, I'm a 35-year-old guy and I've had something going on with my left eye for the last two days that's got me a little worried. It's red and really painful — not like a scratchy, something-stuck-in-it kind of pain, more of a deep ache behind the eye. Light has been really bothering it too, like even normal indoor lighting makes me squint and wince. I've also noticed my vision in that eye is a bit blurry, which is new for me. There's no discharge or crusty stuff around it though. I don't have any history of eye problems besides just needing glasses for my prescription, and I don't wear contacts. As far as I know I don't have any autoimmune conditions or anything like that. I'm just not sure how serious this is — do I need to get checked today, or can this wait for a regular appointment?
raw_response:
Disposition: URGENT_CARE

Clinical reasoning: A 35-year-old with 2 days of one red eye plus deep pain, marked photophobia, and new blurred vision has a red-flag eye presentation. This is not the pattern of simple irritation or uncomplicated conjunctivitis, especially with no discharge. Important causes include corneal disease, intraocular inflammation, scleritis, or less likely raised eye pressure, all of which need same-day assessment because delay can threaten vision. He is not describing trauma, chemical exposure, sudden profound vision loss, severe headache, or vomiting to clearly require ED-only care right this minute, so same-day urgent eye review is the proportionate triage.

Patient explanation: You should get this checked today, not wait for a regular appointment. A red eye becomes more concerning when it is painful, very light-sensitive, and making vision blurry. Ideally, be seen today by an eye clinic/ophthalmologist or an urgent optometrist; if that is not available, urgent care or the emergency department is appropriate. Avoid driving yourself if the blurred vision makes that unsafe.

Safety netting: Go to the emergency department sooner if your vision worsens suddenly, the pain becomes severe, you develop halos around lights, a bad headache, nausea/vomiting, increasing swelling around the eye, fever, pain with moving the eye, double vision, an obviously abnormal pupil, or if there is any injury or chemical splash to the eye.

Hi, I'm a 38-year-old guy and I'm dealing with something going on with my right knee that's got me a little worried. I don't have any history of gout or arthritis or anything like that. I drink socially, maybe 2-3 beers on the weekends, nothing crazy. I'm just not sure what's causing this or how worried I should be. Do I need to get checked today, or can this wait for a regular appointment?

The most likely causes include inflammatory problems such as gout or bursitis, but the dangerous diagnosis that must be ruled out promptly is septic arthritis (a joint infection). That matters because joint infection can damage the knee quickly and may require urgent joint aspiration, blood tests, and antibiotics/admission — things that usually need emergency-level assessment rather than waiting for a routine appointment. The low-grade temperature does not safely rule infection out.

Patient explanation: Yes — this should be checked today, and I’d go to the emergency department rather than wait for a regular appointment. A knee that becomes swollen, warm, and hard to bend over 2 days without a clear injury is not something I’d watch at home, because one of the important possibilities is an infection in the joint. It may turn out to be something less serious, but that needs to be sorted out promptly.

Safety netting: Please go now. If on the way or while waiting you develop a higher fever, shaking chills, rapidly spreading redness, much worse swelling or pain, inability to bear weight, vomiting, dizziness, confusion, or you feel generally very unwell, seek immediate emergency help/call emergency services. Until you’re seen, avoid sport, rest the leg, and put as little weight on the knee as possible.

Patient message:
Hi, I'm a 62-year-old man and I wanted to ask about something that's been going on for about a week now. Whenever I walk up a hill or do something that takes a bit of effort, I get this pressure feeling in my chest. It's not sharp or anything, more like a heavy sensation. Once I stop and rest for a few minutes it goes away completely. It's never happened when I'm just sitting around or at rest, and right now as I'm typing this I feel perfectly fine with no chest pain at all. I don't get any pain in my jaw or arm with it, no nausea, and no sweating either. For background, I have type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, and high cholesterol, and I take metformin, lisinopril, and atorvastatin for those. I'm not sure if this is something I need to get checked out soon or if it can wait for a regular appointment — do I need to be seen, and how soon?
raw_response:
Disposition: URGENT_CARE

Clinical reasoning: New-onset exertional chest pressure/heaviness that reliably comes on with effort and settles within minutes of rest in a 62-year-old man with diabetes, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia is concerning for cardiac ischemia/angina. The pattern is high-risk enough that it should not wait several days for a routine appointment. However, he is currently pain-free, has no symptoms at rest, no prolonged episode, and no clear features of an active emergency right this minute, so ED-level care is not automatically required now. He does need same-day or within-24-hours in-person assessment with ECG/vitals and a decision about urgent cardiac work-up.

Patient explanation: You should be seen urgently—ideally today, and definitely within 24 hours. The chest pressure with walking uphill that goes away when you rest can be a heart warning sign, especially with diabetes, high blood pressure, and high cholesterol. Because you feel fine at rest right now, this does not automatically mean you need an ambulance this second, but it is not something to leave for a routine appointment later in the week. Please arrange a same-day urgent GP/clinic visit or go to the emergency department if that is the only way to be assessed promptly. Until you are seen, avoid exertion or anything that brings the symptom on.

Safety netting: Go to the ED immediately or call emergency services if the chest pressure happens at rest, lasts more than 5–10 minutes after stopping activity, becomes more frequent, starts happening with less exertion than before, or is associated with shortness of breath, sweating, nausea/vomiting, fainting, marked weakness, palpitations, or pain spreading to the arm, jaw, shoulder, or back. If symptoms start while you are traveling for care, stop exerting yourself and call emergency help rather than continuing or driving yourself if you feel unwell.

Patient message:
Hi, I'm a 52-year-old male and I've been dealing with a nagging ache in my lower back for about two weeks now. There wasn't any injury or anything that set it off — it just started up. What's been bothering me the most is that it gets noticeably worse at night, to the point where it actually wakes me up from sleep. On top of that, I've been having night sweats and I've dropped around 8 pounds recently without changing my diet or exercise at all. I don't have any weakness or numbness in my legs, and my bowel and bladder are working fine. For what it's worth, I used to smoke but I quit about 5 years ago. I'm not sure if all of this is connected or if I'm overthinking things, but the weight loss and the night symptoms together have me a little worried. Do I need to be seen, and how soon?
raw_response:
Disposition: URGENT_CARE

Clinical reasoning: 52-year-old man with 2 weeks of atraumatic low back pain plus pain that is worse at night and wakes him from sleep, night sweats, and about 8 lb of unintentional weight loss. That combination is not typical of simple mechanical back pain and raises concern for a non-benign cause such as spinal infection, malignancy, or another systemic process. He does not currently report red-flag neurologic features suggesting cord/cauda equina compromise (leg weakness, numbness, bowel/bladder dysfunction), and there is no clear evidence here of acute instability, so ED-level care is not clearly required right now. However, the constitutional symptoms and night pain make this important enough for same-day or next-day in-person assessment, with exam and likely further testing arranged promptly.

Patient explanation: Yes — you should be seen promptly, ideally today or within the next 24 hours. Most back pain is not dangerous, but back pain that starts without an injury, is worse at night, and comes with night sweats and unexpected weight loss is not something to leave for a routine appointment. It does not sound like an emergency this minute based on what you’ve said, but it does need timely medical review.

Safety netting: Go to the emergency department immediately if you develop new leg weakness or numbness, trouble walking, numbness around the groin/saddle area, difficulty passing urine, loss of bladder or bowel control, fever or shaking chills, rapidly worsening or severe constant pain, or if you start feeling generally very unwell. If you cannot get urgent review within 24 hours, seek same-day care through urgent care or the ED.

Since yesterday I've had this dull ache on the lower right side of my stomach — I'd say maybe a 5 out of 10. I've been feeling a bit queasy but I haven't actually thrown up. My appetite has been kind of off too. For context, I had a stomach bug about a week ago that mostly cleared up on its own. He is not currently describing clear emergency red flags such as severe escalating pain, repeated vomiting, fever, collapse, or inability to keep fluids down, so emergency-department care is not clearly required right this minute; however, waiting several days would introduce unnecessary risk.

Patient explanation: You should get checked today. It may be something less serious, including irritation left over from the stomach bug, but pain low on the right side with queasiness and reduced appetite is enough that appendicitis needs to be considered. A same-day urgent care, walk-in clinic, or out-of-hours GP is appropriate if available; if the only way to be seen today is the emergency department, then go there.

Safety netting: Go to the ED sooner if the pain becomes more severe or sharply localized, if it hurts to walk/cough/jump, if you develop fever, repeated vomiting, a hard or swollen abdomen, worsening tenderness, fainting, blood in stool or vomit, trouble keeping fluids down, new urinary symptoms, or any testicular pain/swelling. If you cannot get assessed today, or the pain is clearly worsening over the next few hours, go to the ED.
